title: Harness Engineering
text:
Preface
This is a hands-on course about the machine around the coding agent. You build that machine step by step. While you build it, the agent builds a full-stack application for you: a .NET 10 backend, an Angular frontend, and tests at three levels. You will type very little of that application yourself. Instead, you type the rules, the checks, and the feedback loops that decide whether the agent’s output is acceptable.
Every command and every prompt in this book ran end-to-end against the same agent and the same model that run in your container. Nothing here is a sketch of what should work. If something behaves differently on your machine, write it down and bring it to class.
The book cannot promise that your agent writes the same code as the examples in these pages. Those outputs are examples, not a guarantee. The chapter “Your run will differ” explains why: it’s a property of the tool, not a flaw in the book.

title: 1  From coder to harness engineer
text:
1.1 You type a prompt, and then you hope
You have all used a coding agent by now. You type a prompt and the agent writes code. Then you hope. Maybe you skim the diff. Maybe you start the app once and click around. Some days you just commit it.
Nothing in that loop tells you whether the code works. The agent is not the problem here. Coding agents write reasonable code a lot of the time. The trouble is that “a lot of the time” is a statement about odds. You never see which of today’s changes fell on the wrong side of those odds.
Hoping does not scale. Reading every line by hand does not scale either. The agent produces changes faster than you can read them, and after the fourth file, you stop paying attention.
crumbs: 1  From coder to harness engineer

title: 1  From coder to harness engineer
text:
1.2 What your job is now
So stop thinking of yourself as the person who writes the code. You are a harness engineer now.
A harness engineer sets the guardrails and the quality gates. You decide the architecture and write the rules that everybody follows. You also decide what “done” means before anyone starts. Then you coordinate a team of agents the way a team lead coordinates people. The team members work in parallel and never get tired. But they also never tell you when they are unsure. They do the typing.
That sounds like a demotion until you look at what is left over. Every hard part of software is still yours. You decide what to build, choose the structure it lives in, define correct behavior, and prove that the thing in front of you actually has it. Only the mechanical part moved.
crumbs: 1  From coder to harness engineer

title: 1  From coder to harness engineer
text:
1.3 Agentic engineers, not vibe coders
“Vibe coding” is the popular name for the other way of working. You describe roughly what you want and take whatever comes back. Then you keep prompting until the app looks like it works. It is fun for a weekend demo. It falls apart the first time somebody has to change the result, because nobody, including you, can say what the code is supposed to do.
You are an agentic engineer instead: same tools, different starting point. You know what you want before you type, and you can put it into words precise enough for an agent to act on. Over a single day you move between four familiar roles.

Coordinator, splitting work into pieces an agent can finish in one go.
Reviewer, reading the diff and the gate output and deciding what ships.
Software architect, fixing the structure so the agent has somewhere to put things.
Product owner, saying what the software has to do and how you will know.

None of those roles is new. What changed is the fifth role, the one where you sit and type the implementation. That role has largely gone away.
crumbs: 1  From coder to harness engineer

title: 1  From coder to harness engineer
text:
1.4 Probabilistic models, deterministic tools
A large language model, or LLM, samples an answer instead of computing one. Ask the same question twice, and you get two different files. Both are plausible, but sometimes only one of them is correct. That is not a bug you can configure away. Sampling is how the model works.
Two habits follow from that, and this whole course is built on them.
Be specific wherever you care about the specifics. Every detail you leave out is a detail the model picks for you. It picks a fresh one every run. If the project has to use one HTTP client, say so in writing. If test files belong in a certain folder, say so. Vagueness is a coin flip, not flexibility.
Put deterministic tools in the path. A formatter has exactly one correct output for a given file. An analyzer either finds the rule violation or it does not. A test suite passes or fails. It gives you an exit code you can act on. These tools never negotiate, and they behave the same way every time. They also do not care how confident the agent sounded. The model supplies the variety. The tools cut away the part of that variety you refuse to accept.
crumbs: 1  From coder to harness engineer

title: 1  From coder to harness engineer
text:
1.5 What a harness is
Harness engineering is the discipline of building the environment around the agent. It makes good output likely and bad output impossible to miss. The agent is the engine, and the harness is everything else.







Harness element
What it does




Context
Which documents and rules the agent sees (AGENTS.md, skills)


Tools
What the agent can reach: a documentation CLI, the package manager, the database


Gates
Deterministic checks the code has to survive: formatter, analyzer, tests


Feedback loops
How a failed gate gets back to the agent by itself (a pi extension)



The harness has one rule: never trust the agent. You verify its output, and then you automate the verification. A check you have to remember to run is a check you will skip on the day you are in a hurry.
crumbs: 1  From coder to harness engineer

title: 1  From coder to harness engineer
text:
1.6 The three mechanisms
Three mechanisms carry most of the harness you are about to build. Each one gets a full part of the course later, so one sentence each for now.
AGENTS.md. A markdown file in the project root. The agent reads it before it starts working. It holds the rules, the folder layout, and the commands that are true for this project and no other.
Skills. Folders of instructions. The agent pulls them in only when the task matches. That keeps a long procedure available without paying for it in every single request.
Extensions. Code the harness runs by itself at fixed points in a session, for example when the agent finishes a run. A failing gate then turns into something the agent has to deal with, not something you happen to notice.
crumbs: 1  From coder to harness engineer

title: 1  From coder to harness engineer
text:
1.7 The application you build
Everything in this course is built around one deliberately dull CRUD application. CRUD means the app does little more than create, read, update, and delete records. That is on purpose. When the domain is boring, all the interesting difficulty sits in the harness. That is the part you are here to learn.

Backend. .NET 10 with ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs, EF Core, and PostgreSQL, with migrations applied on startup.
Frontend. Angular. It reaches the backend through one hand-written API service. That service reads with the httpResource API.
Tests. xUnit for the backend and Vitest for the frontend. Playwright drives the end-to-end tier.

Six steps build that up, in order: the backend skeleton, the first deterministic gate, and a database with integration tests and a gate for the migrations it generates. Then comes the Angular frontend with its own toolchain, a skill that teaches the harness a procedure, and linting as the final stage of the gate.
The next chapter introduces the two pieces of the setup you do not build yourself: the coding agent and the model behind it.
crumbs: 1  From coder to harness engineer

title: 2  Your toolkit
text:
2.1 The pi agent
The coding agent for this course is pi, an open source agent you run in a terminal. It is deliberately minimal. Out of the box it reads and writes files, edits them, and runs shell commands. That is close to the whole list. Anything beyond that, you add yourself through skills, extensions, and configuration.
That minimalism is exactly why the course uses pi. In a bigger agent, half the harness is already there, hidden behind a settings screen. You never find out what it does or why. With pi, you add every rule the agent follows and every check it has to survive yourself. All of it lives in a file you can open.

title: 2  Your toolkit
section: 2.2 The model: GPT-6 Luna through Novedu
text:
2.2 The model: GPT-6 Luna through Novedu
Behind pi sits the model that does the actual thinking. In this course, that model is GPT-6 Luna from OpenAI. Luna is the fast, low-cost model of the GPT-6 series, one step below GPT-6 Sol. Your school’s Novedu platform passes every request from pi on to OpenRouter, a service that sells access to models from many vendors through one account.
Be clear about the trade-off. Out in industry, engineers run stronger models inside far more capable harnesses. The models include Opus, Fable, GPT-6 Sol, DeepSeek, and Kimi. The harnesses include Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor. Those combinations take on work packages far bigger than the steps in this course: a refactoring across 40 files, a migration to a new framework version, a bug report with only a stack trace. When you judge what agentic engineering can do, judge it by those, not by the setup in your container.

title: 2  Your toolkit
section: 2.3 Why a low-cost model is good for learning
text:
2.3 Why a low-cost model is good for learning
Your key costs you nothing. Every request still costs your school money, because OpenRouter bills the school for each token Luna reads and each token it writes, its thinking included.
Cut the work into small steps anyway. A task cut into pieces the agent can finish in one turn is easier to check, and cutting work into those pieces is the skill this course trains. A capable model lets you skip that practice. It absorbs a sloppy prompt, and you never find out what the prompt was missing.
Mistakes are cheap. Luna is the low-cost model of its series, so a failed run costs the school little and costs you nothing. Break things on purpose and watch the gate turn red. Then you run it again. Much of this course is exactly that.

title: 2  Your toolkit
section: 2.4 What you need on your machine
text:
2.4 What you need on your machine
Docker with Compose. On Windows and macOS, install Docker Desktop, which brings Compose with it. On Linux, install the Docker engine plus the Compose plugin from your distribution or from Docker’s own repository.
Visual Studio Code (VS Code). You attach it to the running container and work inside that container’s terminal. Nothing in this course installs .NET, Node.js, or PostgreSQL on your own machine.
You have learned about Docker and VS Code fundamentals in other courses. If you struggle, ask your teacher or an AI. Figuring out how to work with the course material is part of the exercise.

title: 2  Your toolkit
section: 2.5 The project folder from your teacher
text:
2.5 The project folder from your teacher
Your teacher hands you a folder with four files and one subfolder in it. You do not have to write any of them.

compose.yaml defines the two services you work with, the development container and a PostgreSQL database.
Dockerfile builds the development container, with .NET 10, Node.js, the Angular CLI, git, the PostgreSQL client, and pi already installed.
models.json tells pi which model to talk to, where that model is hosted, and how much room it gets. The chapter “Meet pi” reads those numbers with you.
auth.json.example shows the shape of the credential file, with a placeholder where your own key goes.
skill-source/ holds the custom skills for this course. The container sees it read-only as ~/skill-source, and the chapter “The cutoff problem” installs the skills from there into your project.

pi reads auth.json, not the example. That file is missing on purpose, because the key in it is yours alone. The next section gets you that key and turns the example into the real file.

title: 2  Your toolkit
text:
2.6 Pick up your key
The model endpoint is a Novedu coding activity, and you fetch your own key from that activity’s page.






Your coding agent



Sign in with your school account and the page gives you a key of your own. That key is what your coding tool needs. The code below opens the page and nothing else.
Your teacher sees that you asked for a key, never what you ask the agent.

▶ Get your coding key on app.novedu.at



The page also names a server address and a model, and you already have both in the models.json from your teacher. So the key is the only thing you take away from it. In the folder your teacher gave you, copy the example file:
cp auth.json.example auth.json
Then open auth.json and paste the key in place of the placeholder:
{
  "novedu": {
    "type": "api_key",
    "key": "nvk-your-own-key-goes-here"
  }
}
Every key starts with nvk-, so a value in a different shape is the wrong string.






The key is yours



Treat the key like a password. Do not post it anywhere, and never commit auth.json to a repository you push. Nobody else in the class has your key, so a key that turns up somewhere else came from you. Opening the page a second time hands you the same key back, so there is nothing to lose and nothing to rotate.


If you are not a student with access to Novedu, you can still take the course. Point pi at GPT-6 Luna through your own OpenRouter account, or at any other model you have access to.
The next part walks you through starting the container and attaching VS Code. Then you run pi for the first time.

title: 3  Start the container
text:
3.1 Start the two services
Everything in this course runs inside a Docker container. Your own machine stays clean. Everyone in the room gets the same .NET SDK and Node.js, plus the same coding agent. When something breaks, it breaks the same way for everyone. That is what makes the exercises in this book checkable.
Open a terminal on your own machine and go to the folder that holds compose.yaml. Make sure the auth.json you wrote in the toolkit chapter sits in that folder too. Docker mounts it into the container without checking that it exists. When it is missing, Docker creates an empty directory under that name, and pi later fails with a confusing configuration error instead of a plain “key missing”.
Then run:
-d puts the containers in the background. --build builds the image the first time and rebuilds it whenever the Dockerfile changes. That first build downloads the .NET SDK, Node.js, and the agent, so it takes a few minutes. Every later start takes seconds.
Two services come up.
dev. Ubuntu with .NET 10, Node.js LTS, the Angular CLI, the pi coding agent, git, gh, and the PostgreSQL client. This is the machine you work on for the rest of the book.
db. PostgreSQL 18, reachable from dev under the host name db. You do not touch it until the part about the environment. It only has to be running.
Check that both containers are actually up:
You want dev running and db healthy. The db service has a health check in compose.yaml, and dev waits for it. So when dev refuses to start, look at db first.

title: 3  Start the container
text:
docker compose up -d --build





docker compose ps







Read the Dockerfile



The Dockerfile lists every tool the container installs. You can read it yourself or ask an AI to explain it. Nothing in the file is secret, so a free, public AI service is fine.

title: 3  Start the container
text:
3.2 Attach VS Code

Install two VS Code extensions. Container Tools (ms-azuretools.vscode-containers) adds the Containers view. Dev Containers (ms-vscode-remote.remote-containers) attaches VS Code to the container.
Open the Containers view, right-click the running dev container, and choose Attach Visual Studio Code. A new window opens, connected to the container.
In that window, open a terminal. You are root inside the container now. You type every later command in this book there, unless a step says otherwise.







Do not use docker exec



docker exec from your host gives you a shell, and nothing else. There is no editor on the container’s files and no debugger. VS Code extensions do not work in a plain shell. Every command in this book assumes the attached VS Code terminal, so attach once and stay there. You can still experiment with docker exec if you want. If you break things, run docker compose down and docker compose up -d to get fresh containers. Leave the -v off, because that flag also throws away the database and the folder you build the project in.


What you have now is an editor, a terminal, and a debugger all pointed at the container’s filesystem. When the agent writes a file, you open it in the same window. Nothing gets copied between two machines.

title: 4  Meet pi
text:
4.1 Start pi for the first time
pi is the coding agent you drive for the rest of the book. The toolkit chapter explains why it ships with so little. This chapter starts it and checks that it reaches the model.
In the terminal of the attached VS Code window:
~/work is the folder you build the whole project in. Start pi from inside it, because the agent works in the folder you launch it from.

title: 4  Meet pi
text:
mkdir -p ~/work && cd ~/work
pi

title: 4  Meet pi
text:
4.2 Check the credential
pi needs two files to talk to the model. models.json says where the Novedu endpoint is and which model to ask for. auth.json holds your personal key. Both sit next to compose.yaml on your machine, and the compose file mounts them into the container. Because the key lives on your machine, it survives docker compose down and every rebuild.
When pi reports an authentication error instead of answering, open the auth.json next to compose.yaml. Check the JSON shape against the toolkit chapter, and check that the value starts with nvk-. An activity code pasted in there gets you the same error and no hint about why. After you change the file, restart the container, because Docker mounts files at startup. A key that starts with nvk- and still gets rejected means your teacher has closed the activity.
Now type a message and press Enter. Anything will do. You are checking one thing: whether a reply comes back at all.






When pi just sits there



The model runs on a shared endpoint, and a request sometimes never comes back. There is no error and no retry. The session hangs before it prints anything. That happens on roughly one run in two.
If nothing has shown up after about three minutes, press Escape (or Ctrl+C) and send the same prompt again. It is not your prompt and it is not your machine. A retry almost always works.
You can spot a stall instead of slow work by checking whether anything is happening at all. A working agent prints tool calls as it goes. A stalled one has printed nothing since you hit Enter.
The failure also shows up a second way: sometimes the request does come back, after a minute or two, as an empty reply. No error, no text, the prompt line just returns. Treat it the same way as a hang. Send the same prompt again.

title: 4  Meet pi
text:
4.3 The two numbers in models.json
Open models.json next to compose.yaml and read the model entry. Two of its properties decide how much room the agent gets.
contextWindow is how much the model can read in one request, counted in tokens. It covers the whole session so far, including every file the agent opened along the way. Here it is set to 272000.
maxTokens caps a single answer, and it is set to 128000. That is the most GPT-6 Luna writes in one answer, so you will not run into it by accident.
contextWindow sits far below the 1,050,000 tokens GPT-6 Luna can read, and that is a cost decision. Every turn sends the whole session to the model again, and OpenRouter charges more per token once a request is longer than 272,000 tokens. pi compacts a session, summarizing the older messages into a shorter one, as soon as the session gets within 16384 tokens of contextWindow. With the window at 272000, compaction starts before the session reaches the higher price. A single turn that reads several large files can still carry one request past it.
That matters when a turn goes wrong. An agent that has forgotten an instruction you gave five prompts ago has filled its context window, and the compaction summary left that instruction out. Look at what filled the window, not at the numbers in this file. Managing that budget starts in the part about context.

title: 4  Meet pi
text:
4.4 Commands and keys worth knowing







Command or key
What it does




pi
Start an interactive session in the current folder


pi -c
Continue the previous session


pi -p "prompt"
Run one prompt without the interactive interface, for scripting; this book never uses it


/help
List the slash commands


/new
Start a new session with an empty context window


/compact
Summarize the conversation so far into a shorter one


/resume
Pick an earlier session and continue it


!<command>
Run a shell command yourself, without leaving pi


Escape
Abort the current turn


Ctrl+D
Exit pi when the input line is empty



!<command> is the one people forget. You stay in the session and run ls or git diff yourself. You see the real output instead of asking the agent what it thinks is in the folder.

title: 5  Your run will differ
text:
5.1 The agent picks the names
Read this chapter once now. Remember it every time an output block in this book does not match your screen.
The agent decides most names. Two runs of the same prompt produce different class names, different file names, sometimes a different test runner. Where a name has to be stable, like the project layout and the gate script, this book pins it in the harness. You will see exactly how that works.
So sooner or later, a command fails with “no such file.” Sometimes an output block does not match what is on your screen. Three rules cover that.

title: 5  Your run will differ
text:
5.2 Output blocks are “something like this”
Every output block in this book is “something like this”, never a promise. The strings that are quoted are quoted for a reason. Later in the course, you build a script whose last line is QUALITY GATE: GREEN or QUALITY GATE: RED. Both you and the harness read that exact text at the end of the log. Those words are stable, and they matter. The number of tests printed in the same log does not matter.

title: 5  Your run will differ
text:
5.3 Substitute your own paths
When the book says dotnet build backend/Calculator.Api/Calculator.Api.csproj and your project sits somewhere else, use your path. Find the real one with ls and git status before you decide something is broken. grep -rn searches inside files when you need it.

title: 5  Your run will differ
section: 5.4 A verdict that disagrees is a finding
text:
5.4 A verdict that disagrees is a finding
A verdict that disagrees with the book is a finding. A transcript that disagrees is noise. If the book says the gate turns red and yours turns red, the exercise worked. It does not matter how differently your log is worded. If the book says the gate turns red and yours stays green, stop and investigate. That is a real difference. It usually means a check is not wired up the way you think.
The book is not being vague. You are working with a nondeterministic tool, so you check behavior, not appearances.

title: 6  Git is your undo button
text:
6.1 Initialize the repository
An agent run can go wrong. The first one is the most likely to. So build the safety net before you need it, not after.
Set the identity too. A fresh container has none, so the agent’s first commit fails with Author identity unknown and costs you a turn.
Do this now, even though the first prompt in the context part asks the agent to run git init as well. That happens at the end of the run, too late to rescue it, and running git init twice is harmless.
crumbs: 6  Git is your undo button

title: 6  Git is your undo button
text:
cd ~/work
git init
git config user.name "Your Name"
git config user.email "you@example.com"
crumbs: 6  Git is your undo button

title: 6  Git is your undo button
text:
6.2 Commit before, read after
From here on, commit before every prompt and read what changed after every prompt. Use the git CLI, the VS Code Git UI, or any other Git tool you like.
A clean git status before a prompt means everything you see afterwards was written by that one run. The git diff after it is the review. It is the only place where you find out what the agent really did, not just what it says it did in its summary.
crumbs: 6  Git is your undo button

title: 6  Git is your undo button
text:
6.3 Throwing a bad run away
To throw a bad run away you need both of these:
git checkout .      # undo changes to files git already knows about
git clean -fd       # delete the new files the agent created
git checkout . alone is not enough. People often get this wrong. An agent run mostly creates files, and git checkout does not touch anything untracked.
This is throwaway work inside the container, and nobody expects you to push it anywhere. Git here is a safety net and a way to read what changed.






Where your work lives



~/work is not on your own machine, and it does not live inside the container either. compose.yaml backs that path with a named volume called work_data, which Docker keeps outside both. Stopping the containers with docker compose down leaves it alone, and so does rebuilding the image with docker compose up -d --build.
One command does delete it. docker compose down -v removes the named volumes along with the containers, and that takes ~/work and the database with it.
To keep a copy on your own machine, copy the folder out of the container. This one runs in a terminal on your host, not in the attached VS Code window:
docker cp harness-workshop-dev-1:/root/work ./my-harness-work
compose.yaml pins the project name, so the container is called harness-workshop-dev-1 on every machine in the room.
crumbs: 6  Git is your undo button

title: 7  The cutoff problem
text:
7.1 Install the microsoft-docs skill
A model’s knowledge stops at its training cutoff. .NET 10, C# 14, EF Core 10, and the current Angular CLI are all newer than that cutoff, or barely inside it. Ask an agent for “the latest .NET” and you get outdated code that looks right: .sln files instead of .slnx, classic extension methods where C# 14 has extension blocks, and MVC controllers instead of Minimal APIs.
Outdated code is not a prompt problem. Rewording the prompt does not add a fact the model doesn’t have. The fix is to give the agent a way to look things up.
pi in this container can already search the web and fetch pages through a web access extension, and you will sometimes see it do that. A general web search lands wherever the search engine points, current or not. This chapter adds a source you choose: the official documentation, queried directly. Later, AGENTS.md tells pi which source to use for which question. That works because each source is a skill with a name, and pi loads a skill by name.
A skill is a small package of instructions that the agent loads on demand. The microsoft-docs skill teaches pi how to query the official Microsoft Learn documentation.
The command stops and waits for you. It asks whether to install the skill for this project or globally. Choose Project. If you ever want to skip that question, -y picks the defaults.
Two things appear in ~/work afterward:
Open SKILL.md and read the compatibility: line. The skill prefers the Microsoft Learn MCP server. MCP is the Model Context Protocol. It falls back to the mslearn command line tool. pi has no built-in MCP support, so in this container the mslearn command is the one that works.
Run one search yourself before you let pi use the skill:
What comes back is exactly what pi gets to read. If this command fails on your machine, pi has nothing to look things up with. Everything that follows falls back to guessing.

title: 7  The cutoff problem
text:
cd ~/work
npx skills add https://github.com/microsoft/skills --skill microsoft-docs


~/work/.agents/skills/microsoft-docs/SKILL.md
skills-lock.json


npx @microsoft/learn-cli search "what is new in EF Core 10"

title: 7  The cutoff problem
text:
7.2 Install the backend skeleton skills
The microsoft-docs skill tells pi where to find the current API. It says nothing about how your project should look: where the solution goes, what the projects are called, how an endpoint file is built. Those are your team’s decisions, and no public skill knows them. A custom skill is a skill written for one team or one course.
A full ASP.NET Core backend would get a service layer and a persistence project. The calculator has no business logic worth a service, so for now the backend stays one API project plus its tests. That keeps every agent turn small enough to watch what the harness catches. The service layer and the persistence project arrive with the database, in the chapter “Persistence”.
The custom skills come from skill-source/ in the folder your teacher gave you, which the container sees read-only as ~/skill-source. It holds one folder per stage, and pi never reads it. The agent reads only the copies the install puts into ~/work/.agents/skills/. backend-skeleton is the stage you need now.
Install every skill in the backend-skeleton folder into the project:
cd ~/work
npx skills add ~/skill-source/backend-skeleton -y
-y skips the scope question. Since ~/work is a Git repository, the command picks Project on its own. List the skills afterward:
ls .agents/skills/
Next to microsoft-docs, two new folders appear. Each holds a SKILL.md you can read like any other Markdown file. One covers C# style. The other covers Minimal API endpoints, and its examples write the application name as {App}. The skills are written for any application, so they cannot know that yours is a calculator. AGENTS.md supplies that name in the next step.
skills-lock.json now lists three skills. The two new entries say "sourceType": "local", because they came from a folder rather than from GitHub.






Trust the project first



Project-local skills load only after you trust the project. The first time you start pi in ~/work, it asks whether you trust the project. Answer yes. To confirm it worked, start a pi session and ask pi to list its skills. microsoft-docs and the two backend skeleton skills have to appear in the answer. You can also run /skills and check the list.

title: 7  The cutoff problem
text:
7.3 How a skill loads
Open .agents/skills/minimal-api-endpoints/SKILL.md and read the lines between the two --- markers at the top. That header is the skill’s front matter, and it holds a name and a description:
---
name: minimal-api-endpoints
description: "Conventions for ASP.NET Core Minimal API endpoints: endpoint files, TypedResults, error responses, OpenAPI metadata, and their unit tests. Use when creating the API project, adding or reviewing endpoints, or writing endpoint tests."
---
At startup, pi puts the name and description of every installed skill into its system prompt, together with the path to the file. The body below the header stays on disk. The agent reads it only when a task matches the description. So the description costs tokens on every turn, and the body costs nothing until it is needed. That is why a skill can run to a few hundred lines while AGENTS.md has to stay short.
Read how the description ends: “Use when creating the API project, adding or reviewing endpoints, or writing endpoint tests.” That sentence names situations, and the agent compares its task against them. A small model still skips a matching skill now and then, which is why AGENTS.md in the next chapter names each skill together with the task that loads it.
You can also force a skill. pi registers every skill as a command, so typing /skill:minimal-api-endpoints in a session loads that body right away, and whatever you type after the name becomes the request. You will use that later to test a skill you wrote yourself.

title: 8  AGENTS.md
text:
8.1 Why this file works
The skills are installed, but the agent still has to decide to use them. Until it does, pi sees only each skill’s name and one-line description. AGENTS.md is the file pi loads into context at the start of every session. The rules that say which skill to use, and when, belong there. Keep the file short. A long AGENTS.md is an ignored AGENTS.md.
Create ~/work/AGENTS.md and type this into it:
Four rules make this file work.

title: 8  AGENTS.md
text:
It names the skills, and when to load them. The agent now knows the documentation lookup exists instead of guessing from training data that is out of date. It also knows which skill to read before it creates a project, instead of hoping a one-line description catches its attention.
It names the fallback. The Model Context Protocol server the skill prefers is not running in this container. The agent does not waste a turn finding that out.
It states the conventions once, in a file that loads into every session. You never repeat them in a prompt. The agent can’t forget them halfway through the course.
It pins the name and the paths, and leaves the rest to a skill. Commands in later steps depend on exact paths. dotnet build backend/Calculator.Api/Calculator.Api.csproj and bash scripts/quality-gate.sh only work because the agent puts the files where the course expects them. The skill’s layout writes the application name as {App}, and the solution that would tell the agent the real name does not exist before the first prompt. So AGENTS.md, the one file the agent reads on every turn, names the application and the project paths. It also rules out the class libraries a larger backend would get, so the agent keeps the endpoints and their logic in the API project. The folders inside the projects and the naming rules stay in the skill. One of those rules stops a C# trap. Outside its own namespace, the bare name Calculator means the root namespace, even with a using for the class. A class called Calculator turns Calculator.Add(2, 3) in an endpoint into error CS0234.







Why the conventions are so blunt



The rule “never with classic this-parameter extension methods” looks over-specified until you run the same prompt twice. A small model knows the old idiom far better than the new idiom. Without an explicit rule, it falls back to the old one. You get .sln instead of .slnx, and this WebApplication app instead of extension(...). Both compile. Both pass the tests. Only one is what you asked for.

title: 9  The first prompt
text:
9.1 What the prompt leaves out
The microsoft-docs skill gives the agent a way to look things up. The backend skeleton skills describe the project, and AGENTS.md tells the agent when to read each one. Now find out whether the skills and AGENTS.md are enough. Start pi in ~/work and paste this prompt:
The prompt specifies no file layout and no csproj contents. It contains no code and no command lines. It says nothing about .NET versions or idioms. The prompt states the goal and nothing else. The agent works out the rest.
That split is the point. Prompts describe the task, and the harness describes the rules. A rule you put in a prompt applies to one turn. A rule you put in AGENTS.md applies to every turn for the rest of the project.

title: 9  The first prompt
text:
9.2 Watch it work
Watch the terminal for this run, because you will see the agent consult the docs instead of guessing. You should see the agent do most of this:

run npx @microsoft/learn-cli search ... for .slnx files, then for extension blocks and Minimal APIs
run dotnet new and dotnet build, then dotnet test
check package versions against NuGet
possibly start the API and call it with curl

Nobody told the agent about the dotnet new sln --format slnx flag. Nobody showed it what a C# 14 extension(...) block looks like. It read the documentation because AGENTS.md told it to load the microsoft-docs skill. That skill showed it how to query the docs.

title: 10  Review the result
text:
10.1 Run the checks yourself
The agent says it is done and it has committed. Now you check, because a summary written by the agent is not evidence about the agent’s own work.
From ~/work:
The last command matters most. AGENTS.md says every NuGet package reference must be on its latest stable version. The agent will happily tell you it checked. dotnet list package --outdated is how you find out whether that is true. It prints one line per package that has a newer stable version. When everything is current, it names no packages at all.

title: 10  Review the result
text:
git log --oneline
git show --stat
dotnet build backend/Calculator.slnx
dotnet test backend/Calculator.slnx
dotnet list backend/Calculator.slnx package --outdated

title: 10  Review the result
section: 10.2 Find out what the agent built
text:
10.2 Find out what the agent built
The prompt never named the solution, the class that adds two numbers, or the endpoint file. Those names are the agent’s own invention, so yours will differ from your neighbor’s. Read them:
git show --stat
ls -R backend
Then check four properties. Each one is something AGENTS.md demanded. Each one is also something a model trained before .NET 10 gets wrong when nobody stops it.

The projects sit where you pinned them. Two projects side by side, backend/Calculator.Api and backend/Calculator.Tests, and no class library next to them. The Add logic sits in the endpoint file under Calculator.Api/Endpoints, as a method the unit test calls directly. This one is not negotiable, because every command later in the course is written against those paths.
There is exactly one solution file, backend/Calculator.slnx. If you find a .sln, the agent used the format it knows from training. That format is not the one the harness asked for.
The endpoint lives in its own file, not inside Program.cs. Find that file in the git show --stat output.
That endpoint file uses a C# 14 extension(...) block. Open it and look at the signature. You want a block that names the extended type once, in the shape extension(IEndpointRouteBuilder app). The mapping method is written inside it. A method whose own parameter list starts with this is the classic extension method idiom. That means the agent fell back to the old style. It compiles and the tests pass, but it is still not what you asked for.

If a property fails, don’t fix it by hand. Tell the agent what is wrong and let it repair its own output. Patching it yourself hides the failure and teaches the harness nothing.

title: 10  Review the result
text:
10.3 What this step taught you
What went right. Three skills and a handful of lines in AGENTS.md were enough. A small model used them to write current, idiomatic .NET 10 code. The context did the work, not the prompt.
What is still broken. The checks so far do not tell you whether the code is any good.

dotnet build succeeded, which proves the code compiles and nothing else.
The agent told you the tests pass. You are believing a report written by the thing under test.
If you were lucky, the agent called the endpoint with curl. A check that depends on luck proves nothing.
Nothing looked at formatting, naming, or dead code. Nothing checked whether the code follows a single convention, beyond the four properties you just checked by hand.

Every one of those checks currently depends on the agent deciding to run it. That decision is not deterministic. Run the same prompt again and you get a different set of checks. The next part takes the decision away from the agent entirely. Analyzers turn sloppy code into build errors. An extension runs the checks whether the agent wants them or not.

title: 11  Analyzers and a gate script
text:
11.1 What a real gate has to do
Right now the agent decides whether your code gets formatted and whether the analyzers run. It decides whether the tests run too. The same prompt leads to a different decision on a different day. When the agent does run the tests, you learn the result from a summary the agent writes about its own work.
A check that only runs when the agent chooses isn’t a gate, because a gate runs every time. The agent might run it today, but that tells you nothing about tomorrow.
The third requirement matters because a warning is easy to ignore. If a rule violation only prints a yellow line that scrolls past, the agent can honestly report “the build succeeded.” Broken code still sits in the project. Turn the warnings into errors and that sentence becomes impossible to write.
crumbs: 11  Analyzers and a gate script

title: 11  Analyzers and a gate script
text:
It runs every time, without being asked.
It produces a machine-readable verdict, not prose.
It is hard to satisfy by accident. A warning has to be a failure.
crumbs: 11  Analyzers and a gate script

title: 11  Analyzers and a gate script
section: 11.2 One script first, then something that runs it
text:
11.2 One script first, then something that runs it
This part builds the gate in two moves. This chapter gives you a shell script that runs the checks and prints a machine-readable verdict, plus a build that treats warnings as errors. The automation that runs the script every time comes later. The script comes first because a gate that only the agent can trigger is miserable to debug, so it has to work from your shell before anything calls it.
crumbs: 11  Analyzers and a gate script

title: 11  Analyzers and a gate script
section: 11.3 Start this one in a fresh session
text:
11.3 Start this one in a fresh session
Commit first, so git status comes back clean. Then leave pi and start it again, or type /new.
The old conversation is full of dotnet new output and NuGet version lookups from building the skeleton. The agent would carry all of it in its context window through the longest run in the book. Discarding it is safe, because everything the agent needs is in AGENTS.md, the committed code, and git log. None of it lives in the chat.
So here is the rule for the rest of the book: new task, new session. Continue a session while you review what the agent just did or tell it to repair what it got wrong. Start fresh when the task changes.
When a fresh session produces a worse result than a continued one, that is a finding. Something the agent needed was only in the conversation, and it belongs in AGENTS.md instead.
crumbs: 11  Analyzers and a gate script

title: 11  Analyzers and a gate script
text:
11.4 The prompt
Paste this prompt into the fresh session. AGENTS.md already names scripts/quality-gate.sh, so your first run may have left a small script there. That changes nothing, because the prompt defines what the script has to do and the agent extends or replaces whatever is in place.
Add a deterministic quality gate to this project.

1. Turn on .NET code analysis for every project in the solution: recommended
   analysis mode, warnings treated as errors, and all code style rules reported
   as warnings. Look up how to configure this properly.

2. Put the checks into one single script at scripts/quality-gate.sh. That script
   executes, in this order:
     - dotnet format, verify only, must not rewrite files
     - dotnet build
     - dotnet test
   The script must write the combined output to quality-gate.log in the project
   root. The very last line of that file must be exactly `QUALITY GATE: GREEN`
   or `QUALITY GATE: RED`, with nothing after it, so other tools can read the
   verdict. The script exits 0 on green and non-zero on red.

Do not disable or downgrade any analysis rule to make the existing code green.
Fix the code instead. Commit when done.
crumbs: 11  Analyzers and a gate script

title: 11  Analyzers and a gate script
section: 11.5 What the prompt does not contain
text:
11.5 What the prompt does not contain
The prompt carries no MSBuild properties and no .editorconfig rules, and you write no bash in it. It states the requirement, and the agent works out the mechanism from Microsoft’s documentation through the microsoft-docs skill.
Read these two parts of the prompt twice.
The last line of the log file. “Exactly QUALITY GATE: GREEN or QUALITY GATE: RED, with nothing after it” is the machine-readable verdict. Everything you build in the rest of this part reads that string or the script’s exit code.
The ban on downgrading rules. Turning on every style rule makes existing code fail. The fastest way to stop the failures is to switch the rule off. Write that ban into the prompt, or you’ll get a green gate that checks nothing.
Expect this run to take a while, even though a large frontier model would finish it quickly. Treating warnings as errors means that code which built fine a minute ago now has dozens of errors. The agent has to fix every one of them before it can claim success. That’s the gate doing its first run against the code you already have.
crumbs: 11  Analyzers and a gate script

title: 12  Own the configuration
text:
12.1 The build has to turn warnings into errors
The agent just wrote three pieces of harness for you: the MSBuild settings that turn analysis on, the .editorconfig that holds the style decisions, and the gate script at scripts/quality-gate.sh. In a few minutes you’ll trust those three files to tell you whether your code is acceptable. So read them first.
Start by finding out what actually changed:
Open every file in that list. The sections below tell you what to look for in each one. Your files will not match another run’s word for word, and they don’t have to. What has to match is the effect.
MSBuild automatically picks up a file named Directory.Build.props from the folder tree above a project. That makes it the natural place for settings that apply to the whole solution. Look for that file first. If the agent put the properties into the individual .csproj files instead, that works too. You just have more places to keep in sync.
There is more than one correct way to write these settings. Read your file for the four effects in the table, not for the exact property names. AnalysisLevel=latest-recommended and AnalysisMode=Recommended are the same decision spelled differently. “All style rules as warnings” is often a dotnet_analyzer_diagnostic.category-Style.severity = warning line in .editorconfig.
People miss the third row. Style rules are an IDE feature by default. Without EnforceCodeStyleInBuild, your IDExxxx findings never reach the build output, so a gate that runs dotnet build never sees them. If you cannot find that effect anywhere, search for it:
If that grep prints nothing, the gate you are about to turn on is weaker than the prompt asked for. Send the agent back before you continue.

title: 12  Own the configuration
text:
Effect you are looking for
One way to write it




The recommended CAxxxx code-quality rules are on
AnalysisMode=Recommended


All IDExxxx code-style rules are on
AnalysisModeStyle=All


Style rules run during dotnet build, not just in the IDE
EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true


Any warning fails the build
TreatWarningsAsErrors=true




grep -rn "EnforceCodeStyleInBuild\|TreatWarningsAsErrors" --include=*.props --include=*.csproj .

title: 12  Own the configuration
section: 12.2 The editorconfig is where cheating shows up
text:
12.2 The editorconfig is where cheating shows up
.editorconfig holds the concrete style decisions: indentation, brace placement, var usage, and the order of using directives. Microsoft’s C# language rules documentation describes every option in the file. The agent should have read that page while writing it.
It is also the first place to check for cheating:
git diff HEAD~1 -- .editorconfig backend/Directory.Build.props | grep -i "severity = none"
Any severity = none in that diff is the agent deciding which rules you get without telling you. Some of those decisions are fine. Test method names genuinely break CA1707, the rule about underscores in identifiers. Turning it off for the test project is a fair choice. But you make that decision, not the agent, and only after it has told you why. A rule switched off in silence is a rule you will never think about again.






Review the code the agent changed



Read the C# source diff as well as the configuration. The agent may have replaced file-scoped namespaces with block-scoped ones (IDE0160). Look for expression-bodied methods rewritten with block bodies (IDE0022), and var replaced by explicit types (IDE0008).
Decide whether those changes match your team’s preferences. You can keep the style or declare a different preference in .editorconfig. Explain your decision before asking the agent to apply it. A green gate proves the code follows the configured rules; you still have to choose those rules.
Allowing either var or an explicit type requires a separate decision. IDE0007 enforces var, and IDE0008 enforces explicit types. To accept both, disable both diagnostics in the intended scope and explain why.

title: 12  Own the configuration
text:
12.3 The gate script
scripts/quality-gate.sh is the file you will read most often, so read it now while it is small. It runs the three stages in order and writes everything to quality-gate.log.
Check four things in your version.
The format stage only checks. The prompt asked for verify mode, so the script should pass something like --verify-no-changes to dotnet format. A gate that fixes the formatting itself reports green and teaches the agent nothing.
The last line is the verdict, with nothing after it. No timestamp and no row of dashes. In later chapters, other programs read that verdict, and any trailing line breaks them.
The script stops at the first failing stage. You want the first problem, not every failure that follows it. A later chapter relies on the log holding only the stage that failed. If your script runs all three stages whatever happens, send the agent back.
The exit code follows the verdict. Run it yourself and look:
bash scripts/quality-gate.sh; echo "exit code: $?"
Right now, on committed code, it should print 0. Break a file and it has to print something else. The automation you add in the next chapter decides green or red from that number alone. A script that always exits 0 gives you a gate that can never fire.






Why one script and not three commands in the harness



Nothing forces the checks into a script. Whatever runs the checks could run dotnet format, dotnet build, and dotnet test separately. Putting them in one file gives you a single verdict and a single log. You can also run the same gate from your shell and later from a build server. A gate that only exists inside the agent’s session cannot be rerun when it fails.

title: 13  Automate the gate
text:
13.1 What a pi extension is
scripts/quality-gate.sh covers two of the three properties from the gate requirements. It prints a machine-readable verdict, and with warnings turned into errors it is hard to satisfy by accident. Property 1 is still missing. Right now the gate runs when you type its name, and never otherwise.
pi loads TypeScript files from .pi/extensions/ in the project and runs them at session start. An extension subscribes to lifecycle events. When one of those events fires, your code runs inside the agent’s process. It can run shell commands and read files. It can also put a message into the running session.
Other harnesses call the same idea a hook. Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot all let you attach programs to fixed points in a session. The idea is the same everywhere, even though each API is different.
The event you want is agent_end. It fires when an agent run ends. That is the moment pi decides whether it is finished or has more to do. A run is what pi calls one uninterrupted stretch of agent work. A single prompt from you can turn into several runs. That timing is what matters, and it is easy to get wrong.
You won’t write that file. You prompt for it and then read it, which works the same way as everything else in this course.

title: 13  Automate the gate
text:
13.2 The prompt
Commit what you have and start a fresh session, then paste this:
Nothing runs the quality gate automatically. Add that as a project-local pi
extension, written in TypeScript.

What it has to do:

- When your run ends, the extension runs `bash scripts/quality-gate.sh` itself.
- Green gate: nothing happens. No message, no output, silence.
- Red gate: the extension feeds the failures from quality-gate.log back into the
  session as a follow-up user message, and the agent picks the work up again on
  its own and fixes them. Nobody types anything.
- The follow-up message tells the agent to fix the failures and then end its
  turn, without running the gate itself. The extension runs the gate again
  when that run ends.

Rules:

- Hook into the `agent_end` event. `agent_settled` looks like the right one and
  is not: it fires only after pi has decided it will not continue, so a message
  sent from there never starts a new turn.
- Your handler must wait for the gate to finish and send the message before it
  returns. Do not start the gate and return immediately. pi decides whether to
  continue the run from what is queued when the handler resolves, and a handler
  that finishes its work later talks to a session that has already moved on.
- Look everything else up in pi's own documentation. Never guess a function
  signature.
- Do not add any npm package. No new dependencies.
- Do not change scripts/quality-gate.sh.
- The gate takes minutes, so give it a long timeout.
- Keep the injected text small, a few dozen lines of the log at most.

Commit when you are done.

title: 13  Automate the gate
section: 13.3 Two of those rules are not requirements
text:
13.3 Two of those rules are not requirements
Most of the rules are outcomes, the way every prompt in this course states outcomes. The first two are different. They name an event and a control-flow rule, the kind of detail you normally pay the agent to work out.
A small model left to the outcome-only version of this prompt tends to pick agent_settled, or it returns from the handler before the gate finishes. Either way, a red gate then produces no follow-up at all. A larger and more expensive model given the same prompt experiments on its own harness. It picks an event and breaks the gate on purpose to see whether the run continues. When the run stops, it reads the transcript and finds its own mistake.
So every prompt holds two kinds of sentences. Some are the requirement and stay true whatever model you run. Others compensate for the model you happen to use, and you delete them when you move to a stronger one. The two technical rules are the second kind. This course pays that price on purpose, in exchange for a model that fails where you can see it.

title: 13  Automate the gate
text:
13.4 The prompt names no documentation
The analyzer prompt sent the agent to Microsoft’s documentation. This one only says “look everything else up in pi’s own documentation”, with no path and no file name. That is enough, because pi’s system prompt already tells the agent where its own documentation lives and which file covers which topic.
Before you paste a documentation path into a prompt, ask the tool where its manual is. It may already know.

title: 13  Automate the gate
text:
13.5 Read what the agent wrote
git show --stat
ls .pi/extensions/
You should see one TypeScript file. Its name is the agent’s choice. That is why the greps in this section search the whole folder.
The event has to be agent_end. This is the one check you can do with grep. It also decides whether the loop works at all:
grep -rn "pi.on(" .pi/extensions/
One of those calls has to register agent_end, and none of them may register agent_settled. A second handler on session_start that resets a counter is fine. So is the word agent_settled in a comment. You will probably find one there. The prompt named the trap, and the agent tends to write down why it avoided it. agent_settled inside pi.on(...) is the one that matters. Your gate runs and goes red, and no follow-up message appears.
The handler has to be async and finish its work before it returns. Open the file and find the line that registers the handler. A working one reads:
pi.on("agent_end", async (_event, ctx) => {
Then follow the body. The call that runs scripts/quality-gate.sh has to be awaited. The call that sends the message back into the session has to come before the handler returns, not after it in some callback. If the body starts the gate and returns right away, you have the second trap. pi will crash the first time the gate goes red.
The injected text has to be bounded.
grep -rniE "slice|tail|lines|truncate" .pi/extensions/
A working version keeps the last 40 lines of quality-gate.log and throws the rest away. That matters more than it looks. Whatever the extension injects lands in the agent’s context window on the next turn. A build log with a thousand error lines spends the budget the agent needs for the actual fix. If yours pastes the whole file, send it back and ask for a cap.
The message has to tell the agent to stop after the fix. Open the file and read the text the extension sends. It has to say that the agent ends its turn once the failures are fixed, and that the agent does not run the gate itself. “Continue working until the quality gate passes” sounds harmless, but it invites the agent to run the gate as its last action to confirm the fix. Then the run ends, agent_end fires, and the extension runs the whole gate a second time. The extension’s run is the one that counts, so the agent’s run only costs you minutes.

title: 13  Automate the gate
text:
13.6 Extensions load at session start
The file exists and the extension still does not run. pi reads .pi/extensions/ once, at session start. The session that wrote the file started before the file was there.
Leave pi and start it again, or run /reload. Do that after every change to the extension, including the ones the agent makes for you.
Two more things stop an extension from loading. The project has to be trusted. That is the trust prompt pi shows on the first start in a new project. Accept it, or start with pi -a. Project-local extensions only come from .pi/extensions/. An extension the agent decided to put somewhere tidier is an extension that never runs.
You don’t just have to believe this. The next chapter proves the extension is loaded by watching it do its job.






When the session compacts itself



Long runs fill up the context window. pi then summarizes the older half of the conversation on its own. You see it happen in the transcript. Let it finish, and do not abort in the middle of a fix.
/compact triggers the same summary by hand, and you rarely need it. When a run has gone on so long that you want to use /compact, commit whatever is already good. Start the next attempt in a fresh session instead.
The signal to restart is the agent repeating itself, or drifting away from a rule you put in the prompt. A summary keeps the shape of a conversation, but it loses the details. “Do not disable any rule to make the code green” is exactly the kind of detail that goes missing.

title: 14  Close the loop
text:
14.1 An untested gate is worse than no gate
The extension is written and committed. You loaded it into a fresh session. Everything you know about it so far comes from reading it. Reading does not tell you whether it works.
The rule applies to the extension’s two behaviors, and you have to see both. It runs the gate and stays quiet when the code is fine. It puts the agent back to work when the code is not. Test green first, because it is the cheaper experiment.

title: 14  Close the loop
text:
Keep this rule in mind



An untested gate is worse than no gate. It gives you confidence you have not earned. A gate you have never watched fail is a green light with no bulb in it.

title: 14  Close the loop
text:
14.2 Prove the green path first
Commit, so the working tree is clean and the gate is green. Then start pi and give it a prompt with no work in it at all:
Reply with the single word ok. Do not use any tools.
The agent answers ok, and that is the entire session output. You see no gate banner and no verdict line, and the agent never gets a second turn. From the transcript alone you cannot tell whether anything ran.
It is running, though. The gate takes a minute or two after ok comes back, and none of that shows up in the session. Give it that long, then leave pi and look at the log instead:
ls -l quality-gate.log
tail -1 quality-gate.log
The timestamp on the file moved to a few seconds ago, and the last line reads QUALITY GATE: GREEN. The format stage ran, then the build, then the tests. All of that happened on a prompt that did nothing. The harness stayed quiet about it.
Silence is the green state, and that is a design decision you should copy. A message the agent reads on every turn, and can never act on, is noise in the context window. A gate that announces good news is a gate people stop reading.

title: 14  Close the loop
text:
14.3 Break the code by hand
Now make the gate fail. Open the class that adds two numbers. You found its file when you reviewed the first commit in the context part, so go to the same file now.
Indent the return line by four extra spaces and delete the spaces around the + operator. Save it, and leave the working tree dirty.
You break the code by hand rather than asking the agent to write sloppy code on purpose. Models are trained to produce clean code, so they tidy up even when you tell them not to. Ask for broken code and you spend the experiment arguing about whether the code was actually broken.

title: 14  Close the loop
text:
14.4 Read the evidence
Before you let the harness see it, run the gate yourself and read what it says:
bash scripts/quality-gate.sh
tail -30 quality-gate.log
The gate stops at the first stage that fails, the property you checked when you read the script. A formatting break never gets as far as the analyzer or the tests, so the format stage is the one complaining.
Your file names differ from everyone else’s, and so do your line numbers and rule ids. Two properties of the output are the same for everyone.
Every finding carries a file, a line and column, plus the rule that fired. That is machine-readable evidence rather than an opinion. You can grep it and count it. You can also hand it to another program, which is exactly what the extension is about to do next.
Nothing in this log is advisory. A warning is something an agent can report and then ignore. Every line in this log belongs to a stage that failed. That stage failed because the tool it ran returned a non-zero exit code. In the build stage, TreatWarningsAsErrors does the work: a style violation becomes an error, and dotnet build fails. The script stops there.
The last line of the file is the verdict, QUALITY GATE: RED, with nothing after it.

title: 14  Close the loop
text:
14.5 Watch the loop close
Start pi again and send the same empty prompt as before:
Reply with the single word ok. Do not use any tools.
Then take your hands off the keyboard. This one takes several minutes, because the gate runs twice. Watch this sequence happen, with no human input:

The agent replies ok and its run ends.
The extension runs the gate. The verdict comes back RED.
The tail of quality-gate.log goes into the session as a follow-up message.
The agent starts working again, finds the over-indented line and the missing spaces around the +, and fixes the file.
That run ends, and the extension runs the gate again. This time it comes back GREEN.
The session goes quiet, with a clean working tree.

The agent’s last message claims the fix in its own words. Leave pi and check that it is telling the truth:
tail -1 quality-gate.log
git status --short
Stop and appreciate what just happened. Nobody asked for that repair. You did not read the log, and you did not paste it into a prompt. The agent never decided that this change was worth checking. A file in .pi/extensions/ ran a script. The script compared a number to zero, then put the failure back in front of the agent.
Suppose nothing happens after ok, and the log still holds the RED verdict you produced by hand. Then the extension never loaded, or it listens on the wrong event. Restart pi and re-run the grep commands from the “Automate the gate” chapter. A fresh timestamp on the log with no follow-up points to the wrong event. An old timestamp means nothing ran at all.
Suppose instead the log says GREEN while the file is still broken. Then the script is setting the verdict to GREEN before it captures the build output. Re-run bash scripts/quality-gate.sh by hand and read what it wrote.

title: 14  Close the loop
text:
14.6 What the loop costs
The agent does not stop when you think it stopped. A red gate spends another turn and a few more minutes of gate runtime, without you asking for either. On a clean run you never notice. On a bad one you come back to a session that has been arguing with itself.
The repair and the original change land in the same session. You want to read a diff at the point where the agent finished. But by the time you look, two more commits may already sit on top of it. Read git log before you read the code.
A gate that can never go green never stops. The agent sees RED, and the extension sends a follow-up. The agent tries again, but the gate stays RED, so the cycle repeats. The extension needs a hard limit on consecutive retries, a retry ceiling.

title: 14  Close the loop
text:
14.7 The retry ceiling
The loop assumes the agent can fix what the gate reports. Sometimes it cannot. A stopped PostgreSQL container makes the gate go red for a reason that has nothing to do with any line of code. No C# edit will bring it back to green. An extension that answers every red verdict with a follow-up message would sit there retrying until you kill it.
So find out whether your extension has a ceiling:
grep -rniE "max|consecutive|attempt|count" .pi/extensions/
A working extension stops after three consecutive red verdicts. It resets the counter when a session starts, and it shows a warning once when it trips. The prompt did not ask for a ceiling, so your agent’s version might not have one.
If your grep comes back empty, prompt for a ceiling:
The quality gate extension keeps sending follow-up messages as long as the gate
is red, which never ends when the failure is not something the agent can fix.
Add a ceiling: after three consecutive red verdicts, stop sending follow-up
messages and show a warning instead. Reset the counter when a session starts and
whenever the gate comes back green.
Restart pi afterwards, because extensions load at session start.
Three wasted turns and a warning make a bad afternoon. An unbounded repair loop against a stopped database makes a bad week.

title: 15  Tell the agent
text:
15.1 Add the section to AGENTS.md
The agent still does not know that scripts/quality-gate.sh exists. So it invents its own verification, decided fresh every turn: a dotnet build here and a dotnet test there, or nothing at all. Give it the script you own as the entry point instead.
The note also has to say when not to run the gate. If the agent runs it as its last action, the extension runs the whole gate again right after, and every check runs twice.
Type this into AGENTS.md yourself, at the end of the file:

title: 15  Tell the agent
text:
## Quality gate

`bash scripts/quality-gate.sh` runs format, analysis, and tests. The verdict is
the last line of `quality-gate.log`.

The gate also runs by itself when your run ends, from the project-local pi
extension in `.pi/extensions/`. A red verdict comes back to you as a follow-up
message, and you fix it before you are done.

- Run it after an intermediate step of a longer task, to catch problems early.
- Do not run it as your final action. It runs automatically when your run
  ends, and it is slow.






Tell the agent about every automation you add



Each stage you add to the gate is one more check the agent might run by hand, right before the extension runs it again. Whenever you automate something, say in AGENTS.md that it exists and is already handled.

title: 15  Tell the agent
text:
15.2 What this step taught you
The gate now runs after every agent turn, whether the agent wants it to or not. The verdict is a string in a file and an exit code rather than a paragraph of self-assessment. A red verdict comes back into the session and puts the agent back to work. That is a deterministic gate with a closed loop. You built it from one script and one extension, and you never wrote a line of either.
The gate you just built has four gaps.
Nothing prevents a red commit. The gate checks only after the commit already happened. It cannot block anything before that point. When the agent commits and the gate goes red, that commit is already in your history. The loop then fixes the code with a second commit instead of stopping the first one.
The gate is slow. It runs after every turn, even for a one-line change. A full run already takes minutes. EF Core and Angular make the build slower, and Playwright makes the test run longer.
The gate only covers the backend. It skips linting and frontend tests. It has no integration tests and no database.
TreatWarningsAsErrors with every style rule enabled is brutal. It turns every style opinion into a build failure. The rest of the course has to find where a gate that strict costs more than it saves.
Those gaps are the agenda for the rest of the course.

text:
15.3 Where you stand








Harness element
After the context part
After this part




Context

unchanged

mslearn CLI, dotnet, git

All four elements now exist, but none of them is finished. The next part gives the backend a real database. It also gives the gate a fourth stage, one that catches a kind of problem no compiler and no test will ever report. That problem is a generated file that no longer matches the code it was generated from.

title: 16  Persistence
text:
16.1 When the gate grows a dependency
Every stage of the quality gate so far ran on nothing but the source tree: a formatter, a compiler, and unit tests. Hand somebody the repository and the .NET SDK. scripts/quality-gate.sh gives them exactly the verdict it gives you.
A database ends that. The backend now needs a running server before it can serve a single request, and the integration tests run against that server, so the gate needs it running too. From here on, your quality gate can go red for a reason that has nothing to do with your code.
You add this dependency on purpose. Do it now, while the project is still small. At this size, you can trace exactly what the gate needs from the environment.

title: 16  Persistence
text:
16.2 Split the backend into layers
The calculator started as one API project because it had no data to look after. With a database it has rows to store and queries that belong together, and keeping those out of the endpoints is the job of a service layer. The backend grows to four projects. Calculator.Api keeps the endpoints. Calculator.Services gets the business logic, and Calculator.Persistence gets the DbContext, the entities, and the migrations. Calculator.Tests stays where it is.
The rules for that layout come in two more custom skills, from the persistence folder in ~/skill-source. Install them the same way you installed the first two:
cd ~/work
npx skills add ~/skill-source/persistence -y
ls .agents/skills/
Two new folders appear. service-layer says which project owns what, and how an endpoint calls a service. ef-core-postgres covers the EF Core side, down to the flags every dotnet ef command needs once the DbContext lives in its own project.
Installing them is only half the change. AGENTS.md still tells the agent that the backend has two projects and no class library. pi loads AGENTS.md on every turn, while a skill loads only when the agent picks it, so the old rule would win. Open ~/work/AGENTS.md and replace its ## Layout section with this one:
## Layout

- The application is called `Calculator`. The solution is
  `backend/Calculator.slnx`. Next to it sit four projects:
  `backend/Calculator.Api`, `backend/Calculator.Services`,
  `backend/Calculator.Persistence`, and `backend/Calculator.Tests`.
  `.editorconfig` stays in the repository root.
- Before you create a project or write an endpoint, load the
  `minimal-api-endpoints` skill and follow it, with `Calculator` as `{App}`.
- Before you add a service, an entity, or a migration, or run any `dotnet ef`
  command, load the `service-layer` and `ef-core-postgres` skills and follow
  them, with `Calculator` as `{App}`.
- Quality checks live in one script at `scripts/quality-gate.sh`.
The sentence that forbade a class library is gone, and the layout names four projects, because later commands in this part depend on those paths. The new third bullet tells the agent when to load the two new skills. Their one-line descriptions alone are easy for a small model to skip.
Commit the new context before you prompt, so the persistence commit holds only what the agent did:
git add AGENTS.md .agents skills-lock.json
git commit -m "Add the persistence skills and the four-project layout"

title: 16  Persistence
text:
16.3 The prompt
The PostgreSQL server is already running. compose.yaml starts it as the db service. The container you work in gets the connection details as environment variables. Check them before you prompt:
printenv | grep '^PG'
Then give pi this prompt:
Add persistence to the backend.

- Use EF Core with the PostgreSQL server that already runs in this environment.
  Its connection details are in the PGHOST, PGPORT, PGDATABASE, PGUSER and
  PGPASSWORD environment variables of this container.
- Add a `Values` entity with an `Id` and two int properties named `Left` and
  `Right`. The JSON the API accepts and returns uses `left` and `right`.
- Use EF Core migrations and apply pending migrations automatically on backend
  startup.
- Add a new API module in its own file for `Values`, with: create, list all
  (ids only), get by id, and delete.
  - Get by id must also return the sum of the two values, computed with the
    existing `Add` logic.
- Then extend scripts/quality-gate.sh with a stage that fails when the entity
  model has changed but no migration covers that change. Use the command that
  EF Core ships for exactly this check,
  `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes`. It needs no database
  connection, so put the stage where it runs even when the database is down.

Look everything up in the docs. Commit when the quality gate is green.

title: 16  Persistence
text:
16.4 What the prompt pins down
The prompt states outright what no documentation could tell the agent. It names the five PG environment variables, because only this container hands out its connection details that way. It pins the entity name and its two properties, down to the lowercase JSON names. And it makes get by id reuse the existing Add logic instead of adding two numbers a second time.
dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes is pinned for a different reason. A small model asked to “check for missing migrations” tends to write a homemade check instead, a grep over the migrations folder or a trial run of dotnet ef migrations add, and you end up maintaining it. The command ships with EF Core, and naming it costs one line.
Everything else stays open. The ef-core-postgres skill covers the NuGet package and the migration commands, and the agent looks up the rest. Where the code goes is settled by AGENTS.md and the service-layer skill. The DbContext, the entity, and the migrations land in backend/Calculator.Persistence. The Values service goes to backend/Calculator.Services, and the endpoints stay in backend/Calculator.Api.
That split is the point. You tell the agent what exists in this environment and what the result has to be. The documentation covers how to get there, and the gate checks the result afterwards.






The database keeps what you put in it



compose.yaml mounts a named volume for PostgreSQL, so rows survive a restart of the container. Your database is not empty after the first run. Later chapters expect the rows you add now to still be there.


This is a long turn for a small model. Expect the model to work for a while. Expect the gate to run, and sometimes fail, before the agent gets to a commit.

title: 16  Persistence
section: 16.5 A migration is a generated file
text:
16.5 A migration is a generated file
Every file the gate has looked at so far was typed by a person or by the agent. Migrations are not. EF Core reads your entity classes and writes the migration for you. That puts a new kind of file in the repository, and a new kind of failure with it.
A missing migration fails quietly. Add a property to the entity, and forget the migration. The project still compiles, because C# does not know about your database. The unit tests still pass, because none of them looks at the schema. The application starts, sends its first query, and falls over at runtime because the table has no such column. Everything in the repository was green up to that moment.
dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes asks one question: does the current entity model still match the last migration? It answers from the model snapshot that EF Core keeps in the migrations folder. That means it needs no database and no running app. It is fast enough to run after every turn.
That stage does not ask whether the migration is correct; it asks whether the migration is current. Current is the only thing a gate can check about a generated file. A migration that matches the model is wrong only when the model is wrong, and the earlier stages already gate the model.
Every generated file in a project deserves a check of this shape. Lock files, migrations, snapshot tests, and generated code of any kind all share the same weakness. A tool produced them from a source, and nothing notices when the two part ways.

title: 16  Persistence
text:
16.6 Make the new stage fail
Never trust a gate you have not seen fail. The agent has committed and the gate is green, so break the new stage on purpose.
The agent chose the file name and the folder for the entity, so find it first. Open it, and add a third int property next to the other two. Add no migration. Then run the gate by hand:
bash scripts/quality-gate.sh
tail -20 quality-gate.log
The last line has to read QUALITY GATE: RED. Read which stage the failing header names. That is the part you are proving, and your agent wrote the wording of that header itself.
If the analyzer stage goes red first, that is warnings-as-errors reacting to a public property with no documentation comment. Give your new property the same kind of comment its neighbors have and run the gate again. Now the migrations stage is the one that fails.
There are two ways back to green. Running git checkout on the entity file throws the model change away. Adding the missing migration keeps it instead. Take the first one here, since the property was only ever a test. In a real run the agent takes the second one, because your gate just told it exactly what was missing.
git checkout backend/Calculator.Persistence  # adjust to your entity's path
bash scripts/quality-gate.sh                # GREEN again

title: 17  The harness pays off
text:
17.1 Read the commit before you read the code
The agent has committed the persistence work. Before you open a single source file, look at what went into that commit:
Sort that list into two piles.
