One pile is what the prompt and AGENTS.md asked for: the two new projects with the entity, the database context, and the migration files EF Core generated, the Values service, and the new API module. The other pile is everything the prompt does not explain. Read that second pile first. Every file in it is either the harness at work or the agent acting on its own. You want to know which, before you trust the commit.
This commit may have such a file, and it is .editorconfig. Generated code collides with strict style rules. The migration generator writes a byte order mark at the top of each file it produces, and dotnet format --verify-no-changes rejects it. So the gate goes red on code the agent generated but never typed. The extension feeds that failure back into the session. The agent has to deal with it before it can stop. Nobody typed a word about formatting.
That is the harness paying off. Read what the agent decided to do about it:
The fix you want to see is a scoped section that relaxes the rule for the migrations folder and nothing else. Exempting generated code is the one defensible version of “switch the rule off.” The rule from the “Own the configuration” chapter still holds: the agent does not make that call in silence. Check the scope, not just the intent.
Not every run ends up in this exact situation, so your commit may leave .editorconfig untouched. The ef-core-postgres skill tells the agent to run dotnet format right after it generates a migration, and that run may already repair the file before the gate sees it. The two piles still apply. Whatever sits in your second pile, chase it down the same way: the diff, the gate log, or a direct question to the agent. A change nobody asked for is not automatically wrong, but it never gets to stay unexplained.

title: 17  The harness pays off
text:
git show --stat HEAD



git diff HEAD~1 -- .editorconfig

title: 17  The harness pays off
section: 17.2 What to check in the diff
text:
17.2 What to check in the diff
Now read the code. The agent chose the file names and the folder layout on its own, and it named the classes. Start by finding out what it made:
git show --stat HEAD
grep -rn --include=*.cs "MigrateAsync\|Migrate()" backend/Calculator.Api
grep -rn --include=*.cs "PGHOST\|Npgsql\|UseNpgsql" backend
grep -rn --include=*.cs "DbContext" backend/Calculator.Api/Endpoints
Check four properties, and each one tells you where to look.
Endpoints call services. The last grep has to print nothing. An endpoint in Calculator.Api takes a service interface from Calculator.Services and never the DbContext itself. A hit means the agent skipped the service layer for that endpoint, so send it back to the service-layer skill.
Migrations run on startup. Program.cs has to apply pending migrations before the app starts serving requests. It usually does that with a call to MigrateAsync() on the context’s Database facade. Without it, the first request hits tables that do not exist yet.
The connection comes from the environment. The five PG variables hold the connection details. If you find a full connection string sitting in appsettings.json, the agent hard-coded the credentials instead. The prompt told it to read them from the environment. That setup breaks on any machine with a different database.
Get by id reuses the existing logic. The sum in the response has to come from the Add method, which already has unit tests. With the service layer in place, Add moves out of the endpoint file into a service in Calculator.Services. If you find left + right written out a second time inside the new service or endpoint, the agent duplicated that logic. Say so and make it redo that part.

title: 17  The harness pays off
text:
17.3 Try it for real
Reading the diff is not the same as seeing the API work. Start the API in the container shell:
dotnet run --project backend/Calculator.Api/Calculator.Api.csproj
Then, in a second terminal inside the container:
PORT=<the port it printed>
# create one, and keep the id it gives back
ID=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:$PORT/api/values \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"left":17,"right":25}' | grep -o '"id":[0-9]*' | cut -d: -f2)
curl -s localhost:$PORT/api/values          # a list of ids, yours among them
curl -s localhost:$PORT/api/values/$ID      # {"id":…,"left":17,"right":25,"sum":42}
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X DELETE localhost:$PORT/api/values/$ID
That block captures the id from the POST response instead of assuming 1. The database is shared and keeps whatever earlier runs left in it. So the row you just created is almost never the first one.
The field names are the second detail to watch, and they can trap you. If your agent named the JSON fields something other than left and right, the POST does not fail. ASP.NET Core binds the unknown fields to nothing. It cheerfully stores a row of two zeros and returns 200. So check the response body, not the status code. When {"id":…,"left":0,"right":0,"sum":0} comes back, open the API module the agent wrote for Values. Read the names it actually chose. That file also carries the real route if the agent did not pick /api/values:
grep -rn "MapPost\|MapGet\|MapDelete" backend/Calculator.Api --include=*.cs

title: 18  Integration tests
text:
18.1 Install the integration test skill
The rules for integration tests come in one more custom skill, from the integration-tests folder in ~/skill-source:
web-integration-tests appears next to the earlier skills. It covers the packages, the fixture that starts the API, and how a test class cleans up after itself. It also shows how the fixture moves the tests to a database of their own, which the prompt below asks for.
Tell the agent when to load it. Add this bullet to the ## Layout section of ~/work/AGENTS.md, below the one for the persistence skills:
Commit the skill and the new bullet before you prompt:

title: 18  Integration tests
text:
cd ~/work
npx skills add ~/skill-source/integration-tests -y
ls .agents/skills/


- Before you write or change an integration test, load the
  `web-integration-tests` skill and follow it, with `Calculator` as `{App}`.

git add AGENTS.md .agents skills-lock.json
git commit -m "Add the integration test skill"

title: 18  Integration tests
text:
18.2 The prompt
The backend now stores rows in PostgreSQL, and the unit tests still only cover the calculation logic. Nothing yet proves that a request travels through routing, model binding, EF Core, and the database, then comes back correct. That is what this prompt is for:
Add web API integration tests.

- Use the built-in ASP.NET Core support for integration testing. Look up what
  .NET 10 offers for this.
- Add an xUnit fixture that starts the API in-process. Make sure it applies the
  EF Core migrations before the tests run.
- The tests run against their own database on the PostgreSQL server of this
  environment, never against the development database in PGDATABASE. Name it
  after PGDATABASE with `_test` appended. The tests must not assume it is
  empty, and they must clean up whatever they create.
- Add one integration test. It creates a `Values` entity, lists all ids, gets
  it by id and checks the sum, and finally deletes it.

Commit when the quality gate is green.

title: 18  Integration tests
section: 18.3 The bullet that does the work
text:
18.3 The bullet that does the work
The third bullet is the one that changes how the tests have to be written.
First, it keeps the tests out of the development database. The gate runs the tests after every agent turn, and every run creates and deletes rows. In the development database those rows would sit next to the ones you created with curl, and one careless cleanup filter would delete yours too. A second database on the same server costs nothing: no new container and no new credentials, only a different name. With PGDATABASE=appdb the tests use appdb_test. The web-integration-tests skill shows the fixture how to swap the database, so the prompt only has to state the rule.
The test database can still hold rows, though. It outlives a single run, and every test class in a run shares it. Take a test that expects GET /api/values to return exactly one id. It passes when you run it alone. It fails the moment a second test, or a run that crashed halfway, has left a row behind. The test is not wrong about the code; it is wrong to assume the database is empty.
Writing those constraints into the prompt costs one bullet. Finding the problem later, in a test that fails only in a full run, costs an afternoon.

title: 18  Integration tests
section: 18.4 Find the pieces in your own code
text:
18.4 Find the pieces in your own code
The agent picked the file names and the class names again, so go look. Four things should be there, and each one is worth understanding rather than just confirming:
git show --stat HEAD
grep -rn "WebApplicationFactory" backend/Calculator.Tests
grep -rn "_test" backend/Calculator.Tests --include=*.cs
grep -rn "partial class Program" backend/Calculator.Api
head -1 backend/Calculator.Tests/*.csproj
A fixture built on WebApplicationFactory<Program>. This is the built-in ASP.NET Core support for integration testing. It boots the whole application in-process and hands the test an HttpClient wired straight into it. You never pick a port or start dotnet run, and the test reaches the app without curl. Open the fixture and confirm it also applies the migrations before any test runs.
A database of its own. The fixture builds a connection string from the same PG variables as the app, with _test appended to the database name, which is what the _test grep finds. It then replaces the app’s DbContext registration with one that uses that connection string. The first test run creates the database, because applying the migrations creates a missing database first. List the databases on the server to see it next to the development one:
psql -d postgres -c '\l'
If only the development database is there after a green run, the tests ran against it. Send the agent back to the web-integration-tests skill.
The test project can name the entry-point type. Top-level statements compile into an internal class called Program, and WebApplicationFactory<Program> references it from another project. Your agent made that legal in one of two ways. The common one is a public partial class Program {} marker at the end of Program.cs, which is what the grep finds. The other is an <InternalsVisibleTo Include="Calculator.Tests" /> entry in the API project file. If the grep comes back empty, check the .csproj before you send the agent back. A green build means one of the two is in place.
The factory depends on one package. The .csproj under backend/Calculator.Tests references Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing. Besides the WebApplicationFactory class, its build targets copy the API project’s dependency manifest into the test output, and that manifest is what lets the factory boot the real app. Whether the Sdk attribute reads Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web or plain Microsoft.NET.Sdk makes no difference once the package is referenced, so leave that choice to the agent.

title: 18  Integration tests
section: 18.5 Read the count, not the wording
text:
18.5 Read the count, not the wording
Run the gate by hand and look at the test stage in quality-gate.log. The summary looks roughly like this:
Passed!  - Failed: 0, Passed: 10, Skipped: 0, Total: 10
Your wording will probably differ. If the agent picked the newer Microsoft.Testing.Platform runner, the same result reads Test run summary: Passed! with the counts on separate lines. The exact number depends on how many unit tests you already had. What matters is that the count went up and that the failure count is 0.
Unit tests and integration tests both run in the same stage, every time an agent run ends. You never opened scripts/quality-gate.sh for this step. The stage calls dotnet test, and dotnet test found the new tests on its own.
A gate defined in terms of the toolchain grows with the project. A gate defined as a list of test names does not.

title: 19  Break the environment
text:
19.1 Break the environment, not the code
Everything is green and the working tree is clean. Now stop the database and run the quality gate again:
The tail of the log looks about like this:
The exception text depends on your machine and on how far the connection attempt got. The two stable parts are the Npgsql name in the error and the last line of the file, QUALITY GATE: RED.
Nothing is wrong with your code. Not one line of it changed since the last green run. The gate is red because a container is down.

title: 19  Break the environment
text:
docker compose stop db      # from your host, not inside the container
bash scripts/quality-gate.sh
tail -20 quality-gate.log

=== Stage: dotnet test ===
   Npgsql.NpgsqlException : Resource temporarily unavailable
     at Npgsql.Internal.NpgsqlConnector.ConnectAsync(...)
RESULT: FAIL (exit code 1)

QUALITY GATE: RED


docker compose start db
bash scripts/quality-gate.sh   # GREEN again






Where to type docker compose



docker compose stop db runs on your host, in the folder that holds compose.yaml. Inside the development container there is no Docker daemon to talk to, so the command fails there. Everything else in this chapter runs in the container shell as usual.

title: 19  Break the environment
text:
19.2 What red means now
Until this part, a red gate meant the code is wrong. The migrations drift check stretched that a little, since a missing migration is a gap rather than a broken line. Stopping the database stretches it much further. From here on, red means the code is wrong, or something the code depends on is not there. Those two need different reactions. When the code is wrong, read the diff. When a dependency is missing, start the database. A gate that cannot tell you which one you are looking at teaches people to shrug at red. A gate people shrug at is already dead.
Your extension’s retry ceiling exists for this failure. An agent cannot start a stopped container by editing code. Without the ceiling, it would keep trying until you stopped it.

title: 19  Break the environment
text:
19.3 Three things to argue about
Take these to class and disagree out loud about them. None of them has one right answer.
A gate that is slow, flaky, or dependent on infrastructure gets disabled. Not by anybody’s decision, but by attrition. Somebody appends || true to the failing stage on a bad afternoon. Somebody else stops reading quality-gate.log. Six weeks later, the gate is decoration. So what is the honest maintenance cost of the gate you just built, in seconds per turn and in patience per week?
Shared test data breaks when tests run in parallel. Your integration tests pass today because there is one of them and it cleans up after itself. Now imagine ten tests sharing one database, each creating and deleting rows. They collide with each other. What would you change first, and what does that change cost?
The agent’s context is a budget. This step was split into two prompts on purpose. Give a small model EF Core, migrations, four endpoints, and an integration test fixture in a single turn. It tends to do the first half well and the second half badly. The instructions that came first crowd out the ones that came last. Splitting work into coherent chunks is not a workaround for a weak model; it is part of designing the harness. You will do it again for the frontend.

title: 19  Break the environment
text:
19.4 The quiet win
Look at what happened while you were busy with EF Core. You added a database, four endpoints, and an integration test. At the same time, you also added the migrations drift check. It cost one bullet in one prompt, on the day the project had exactly one entity and one migration.
From now on it runs after every turn, on a project that grows entities. Every future change to the model has to arrive with a migration next to it. You have already watched the stage go red when one did not. The cheapest time to build a gate is before you need it.
Next you point the harness at a second toolchain. An Angular frontend brings its own package manager, build, tests, and documentation. The agent has seen none of it. The gate has to grow to cover all of it without becoming too slow to run every turn.

title: 20  More sources of truth
text:
20.1 What a frontend breaks
Everything in your harness so far runs on .NET. NuGet manages packages, and dotnet runs the build and the tests. scripts/quality-gate.sh calls dotnet and nothing else, and the extension runs that script after every agent turn.
An Angular frontend breaks that setup in three ways.
A second ecosystem. npm brings its own build and its own test runner. Your gate script now has to drive two toolchains and still return a single exit code.
A contract nobody generates. The Angular code that calls the backend is hand-written TypeScript. You describe the request and the response a second time, in a second language. No tool compares your description with the C# on the other side. TypeScript accepts both, so a renamed field turns into a surprise in the browser at runtime, not a compile error.
A new kind of test. End-to-end tests need the backend and the frontend running, plus a browser. They are too slow for every agent turn, so you decide which checks belong in which loop.
There’s a fourth problem too. This one is about the model, not your project. pi runs a small model whose training data ends well before the Angular version that ng new installs today. It knows NgModule, and it always uses an observable. It has barely seen the resource API that this course uses for reads. Ask it for a service, and you’ll get 2022 Angular. It compiles fine, but it’s not what you asked for.
So the angular-developer and find-docs skills are not a convenience here. For the backend, microsoft-docs covered a difference of a version or two. For Angular, those two skills are the only place the current API exists at all. Every piece of frontend work in this part depends on the agent actually reading them.

title: 20  More sources of truth
text:
20.2 Four places to find information
Your agent has had exactly one place to look up documentation: the microsoft-docs skill. For Angular work it needs four more. The three commands below install them.
cd ~/work
npx skills add https://github.com/angular/skills
npx skills add upstash/context7@find-docs
npx skills add mattpocock/skills@writing-for-agents
Each command stops and asks whether to install for the project or globally. Choose Project for all three, the same scope you chose for microsoft-docs.
Two of the three arguments use the owner/repo@skill form, and one is a URL. The owner/repo@skill form picks one named skill out of a repository that holds several, so upstash/context7@find-docs installs find-docs and nothing else. The Angular URL has no skill name, so it installs everything that repository offers. Right now, that’s two skills. List the folder to check:
ls .agents/skills/
# angular-developer  angular-new-app  ef-core-postgres  find-docs
# general-csharp-guidelines  microsoft-docs  minimal-api-endpoints
# service-layer  web-integration-tests  writing-for-agents
Ten folders, four of them new. Here is what each new skill does.







Skill
What it is for




angular-new-app
How to create an Angular app with the CLI


angular-developer
Angular architecture: signals, forms, dependency injection, testing, styling


find-docs
Context7, current docs for any library, through npx ctx7@latest


writing-for-agents
How to write documents that an agent reads

title: 20  More sources of truth
text:
20.3 Try find-docs by hand
Never install a skill you have not seen work. Run the tool that the find-docs skill wraps, yourself, before the agent ever calls it:
npx ctx7@latest library Angular
No API key and no MCP server are involved. What comes back is not documentation but a list of candidate library ids, each with a benchmark score. The top one for Angular is /websites/angular_dev, the framework’s own documentation site.
Resolving a name to an id is step one of two. Step two takes the id and a question:
npx ctx7@latest docs /websites/angular_dev "zoneless change detection"
Read what that returns. It’s exactly what appears in the agent’s context window when it uses find-docs. If the output looks incomplete or wrong for a topic, don’t trust the agent’s answer on that topic.

title: 21  Route the docs
text:
21.1 Four overlapping sources need a router
Four documentation sources are worse than one unless the agent knows how to choose between them. Ask about IEndpointRouteBuilder, and Context7 answers right away, with docs that may or may not match your .NET version. Ask Microsoft Learn about Angular signals and you get nothing useful at all. The sources overlap in some places and miss each other completely in others. So routing each question to the right source is now part of your harness.
Part of that routing is already in place. The ## Layout section of AGENTS.md names a project skill for each kind of backend work: minimal-api-endpoints for endpoints, service-layer and ef-core-postgres for services, entities, and migrations, and web-integration-tests for integration tests. Those skills say how this repository does something. The documentation sources answer a different question: what a library offers in the version you have installed. The two can disagree. Microsoft Learn’s Minimal API tutorial injects the DbContext straight into the endpoint handler, which is exactly what your service-layer skill forbids. So the routing also has to say which one wins.
There’s a second problem too. It’s about the file itself. Agents write padded, hedged prose, the kind that reads fine and instructs badly. AGENTS.md is loaded into context on every turn, so a wasted word is paid for again on every turn. The writing-for-agents skill teaches the agent to write a document whose reader is another agent, not a human.
So the prompt below asks for two things at once. Route the documentation sources, and write the routing in a form that costs almost nothing to load. The project skills stay where they are, under ## Layout.

title: 21  Route the docs
text:
21.2 The prompt
Rework the "Up-to-date documentation" section of AGENTS.md.

You now have several documentation sources, and that section must tell you which
one to use when:

- .NET, C#, EF Core, ASP.NET Core: the `microsoft-docs` skill.
- Creating the Angular application: the `angular-new-app` skill.
- Before writing a larger piece of Angular code: read the `angular-developer`
  skill first.
- Any other detail, API signature, configuration option or how-to, for any
  library: the `find-docs` skill (Context7).

The "Layout" section already says which project skill to load for which backend
task. Do not repeat those skills in this section. Add one rule instead: when a
project skill and the documentation disagree, follow the project skill. It says
how this repository does something, and the documentation only verifies the API.

Read the `writing-for-agents` skill first and follow it. AGENTS.md is written for
an agent, not for a human, and it is loaded on every single turn.

Change only the "Up-to-date documentation" section. Leave the ".NET Project
conventions", "Layout" and "Quality gate" sections and every line in them
exactly as they are.
Do not make the file longer than it has to be.
What comes back should be a routing table, not an essay. Roughly this shape:
## Up-to-date documentation

Verify any API, project file property, configuration option or CLI flag in
the docs before using it:

- .NET, C#, EF Core, ASP.NET Core: the `microsoft-docs` skill.
- Creating the Angular app: the `angular-new-app` skill.
- Before writing a larger piece of Angular code: read the `angular-developer` skill.
- Any other library: the `find-docs` skill (Context7).

A project skill named under `## Layout` wins over the documentation. It says how
this repository does something, and the documentation only verifies the API.
Your wording will differ. What matters is that a reader can answer “which skill do I load for this question” right away, without a paragraph of preamble. Backend work hits two lines: the project skill from ## Layout for the shape of the code, and microsoft-docs for the API it calls.

title: 21  Route the docs
section: 21.3 Read the diff, and read it for deletions
text:
21.3 Read the diff, and read it for deletions
You just told an agent to rewrite a file that governs every future turn. Look at what it actually did:
git diff AGENTS.md
Two things to look for.
Did the other sections survive? The prompt names .NET Project conventions, Layout, and Quality gate by their headings and says to leave them exactly as they are. “Keep the existing conventions” is not precise enough on its own. An agent can read “conventions” as “the documentation rules” and then drop your .slnx rule and your C# 14 extension(...) rule. It may still report that it kept everything. A rewrite prompt without an explicit protection clause is a prompt that silently deletes things.
## Layout is the section most at risk here, because its bullets name skills too. An agent asked to route skills likes to pull them into the new section, or merge them into one list. List every line that names a skill:
grep -n "skill" AGENTS.md
The four backend skills still have to sit under ## Layout, each with the task that loads it. The documentation section names microsoft-docs, the two Angular skills, and find-docs. A backend skill showing up there is a duplicate that the next rewrite will let drift apart from its original.
What else disappeared? Read every line the rewrite dropped, not only the ones the protection clause covers. One line that’s likely to disappear is the note “there is no MCP server in this container, so use the CLI fallback.” The microsoft-docs skill documents its own fallback, so dropping that note is defensible. But it was a line you wrote on purpose, and now it’s not there. Decide whether you want it back, and add it yourself if you do. The same question applies to every other dropped line.






When an agent rewrites a file, git diff is not optional



A summary of a rewrite is written by the thing that did the rewriting. It reports what the agent believes it did, not what landed on disk. The diff is the only account of the change that nobody had a reason to polish.

title: 21  Route the docs
section: 21.4 Pin a library id when the agent keeps guessing an old version
text:
21.4 Pin a library id when the agent keeps guessing an old version
The routing table sorts questions by topic. You can route one level deeper and pin a single library. One library in this project has earned it: xUnit. In the quality gate part, the agent lost turns on xUnit v3’s new test runner. A small model knows the old xUnit v2 idioms far better than v3. The v3 answers live on xunit.net, which Microsoft Learn does not cover.
Watch what happens when the agent asks Context7 for xUnit. Run the resolution step yourself:
npx ctx7@latest library xunit
You get four Context7 library ids for the same project. One is the documentation website. Another is a snapshot of the API reference pinned to one v3 release. The last two are mirrors of the GitHub repository. All four look plausible. Which one the agent picks is a fresh decision on every run. By now you know what to do with a decision like that: take it away. Try the website one, with a question you already know the answer to:
npx ctx7@latest docs /websites/xunit_net "what changed in the v3 test runner"
Read a screenful of what comes back. That’s current v3 documentation, the material the model’s training data does not have.
Now pin it. Add one line to the routing list in AGENTS.md, by hand, the same way you added the quality gate section there:
- xUnit v3: the `find-docs` skill with the Context7 library `/websites/xunit_net`.
The same move applies beyond this project. When the model keeps guessing an outdated version of one specific library, pin that library’s documentation source by id in AGENTS.md. It’s the same trick as pinning the folder layout in the first chapter of the course. It turns a choice the agent would otherwise make fresh every run into a choice made once, in the harness.

title: 22  The Angular app
text:
22.1 Pin the frontend layout
The backend got its folders from AGENTS.md and a skill. The frontend has neither yet, so the agent picks a structure on every run. One run puts every file flat in src/app. Another invents a core/ folder and stops there. Each later page lands wherever that first run decided.
A structure exists already. The angular-developer skill recommends one in references/naming-conventions.md: backend access in core/, one folder per feature under features/, and reusable parts with no business logic in shared/. That file is one of about 40 references in the skill, and nothing sends the agent there. So do what you did for the backend. AGENTS.md names the folders, and the skill holds the details. Add these two bullets to the ## Layout section of ~/work/AGENTS.md, at the end:
The first bullet pins the folders that later commands and reviews depend on. The second one sends the agent to the file names and class names, which change with the Angular version and belong in the skill.
Commit the new bullets before you prompt:

title: 22  The Angular app
text:
- The frontend is one Angular application in `frontend/`. Inside
  `frontend/src/app`, the backend calls and their models live in `core/`, each
  page gets its own folder under `features/`, and components, pipes and
  directives with no business logic go in `shared/`.
- Before you create a file in `frontend/src/app`, read
  `references/naming-conventions.md` in the `angular-developer` skill and
  follow it.


git add AGENTS.md
git commit -m "Pin the frontend layout"

title: 22  The Angular app
text:
22.2 The prompt
This one prompt asks for the whole frontend, the service that talks to your backend, and a new gate stage. Most of it is ordinary scaffolding. Two bullets are not, so read them before you paste.
Add an Angular frontend to this repository.

- Create a single Angular application in a `frontend` folder. No library, no SSR,
  no PWA. Standalone and zoneless, with routing but without lazy loading.
- Styling is plain modern CSS using custom properties. Do not add Tailwind,
  Bootstrap or any other CSS framework.
- During development the frontend must reach the backend through a proxy on /api.
- One single Angular service holds every call to the backend: create, list all,
  get by id and delete for the Values entity, plus the add calculation.
- The reads that fetch stored Values (list all, get by id) use Angular's
  httpResource API. Do not write these reads as HttpClient methods that return
  an observable.
- Create and delete use HttpClient, because a resource is read-only. For the add
  calculation, pick whichever of the two fits the endpoint the backend has.
- No component calls HttpClient, httpResource or fetch itself. Components use the
  service.
- Test the service with Vitest, using Angular's HTTP testing support
  (provideHttpClientTesting and HttpTestingController).
- Add npm scripts for the tasks that matter: `start`, `build` and `test`.
- Use the latest stable versions of all npm packages.
- Do not create AI assistant config files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and similar).
  This repository already has one.
- Add a project skill in .agents/skills/api-access/SKILL.md. It documents this
  convention: where the backend calls live, which of them use httpResource and
  which use HttpClient, the development proxy, and when the file has to be
  touched.

Then add a stage to scripts/quality-gate.sh that builds the frontend for
production. Commit when the quality gate is green.
This is a hard run for a small model, harder than the quality gate was. httpResource is newer than the model’s training data, so the agent cannot write a line of the service from memory. It has to read the angular-developer skill or ask Context7 first. Expect several turns, and expect at least one of them to produce observables anyway.

title: 22  The Angular app
text:
22.3 One bullet names the mechanism
Every prompt in this course states outcomes and lets the agent decide how. One bullet here breaks that rule on purpose, twice in two sentences. It names httpResource for the stored-data reads. Then it names the answer you refuse to accept: an HttpClient method returning an observable.
The reason is the model, not the requirement. The model has seen the HttpClient and observable pattern thousands of times, and httpResource almost never. So “read through the modern resource API” reads to it as “make a request somehow.” What comes back then compiles and passes the gate. It shows the right numbers on the screen. So nothing you have built so far can tell you it went the wrong way.
Naming the wrong answer is the cheapest fix there is. It’s also the kind of sentence you’ll delete the day you move to a stronger model. The agent_end rule in the extension prompt is the same kind of thing: written for this model, not for the requirement.






If your agent builds more than you asked for



Some runs of this prompt produce more than scaffolding: a finished calculations page, sometimes a values page too, complete with tests. The next two chapters ask for exactly those pages. So the agent may reply “nothing to implement, everything already exists.” That’s not a problem, so keep the commit and paste the prompts anyway. Treat the chapters as review checklists for pages you already own. Every check in them still applies.

title: 22  The Angular app
section: 22.4 Review the skill the agent wrote
text:
22.4 Review the skill the agent wrote
Everything except the skill bullet asks the agent for application code. The skill bullet asks it to write a piece of your harness. That’s a different kind of work, and it deserves a different kind of review.
Open .agents/skills/api-access/SKILL.md once the run is done. A useful skill states four things.
The one place requests live. It names the path of the service file, inside core/, and states the rule that goes with it: components never make a request themselves.
Which mechanism goes with which direction. Reads go through httpResource. Create and delete go through HttpClient. A resource is read-only by design, so a write cannot go through one.
When the file has to change. The next agent can recognize these situations: a backend endpoint is added, renamed, or removed; a request or response shape changes; or the port behind the proxy changes.
The failure symptom. This is what a broken binding looks like from the outside. The frontend compiles without complaint. Then the request 404s at runtime, or it succeeds and the fields come back undefined, because the TypeScript type and the C# model disagree.
The failure symptom is what separates a skill from a README. A README documents a convention. A skill describes a situation the next agent will find itself in, and it tells the agent what to do about it. So it fixes the cause, instead of debugging the symptom for half an hour.
One way to write the two parts that matter:
---
name: api-access
description: How the Angular frontend talks to the .NET backend. Every request
  goes through the single API service; reads use httpResource, create and delete
  use HttpClient, and /api is proxied to the backend in development. Use when
  adding or changing a backend call, when a backend endpoint or model changes,
  or when a request fails at runtime.
---

## Failure symptom

The frontend compiles and still gets it wrong: the request 404s, or fields come
back undefined because the TypeScript type and the C# model disagree. Nothing
before the browser or the Playwright suite catches this.
Yours names the real path of your service file. The description above leaves that open, because the agent picked the path. Compare the rest with what your agent produced, and spend most of your attention on the description. Everything under the front matter is loaded only when the agent decides the skill is relevant. The agent reads the description on every turn and uses only that field to decide whether to load the skill. If the description says “documentation about the API service,” the agent never loads the skill on the turn where it adds an endpoint. That one field is worth arguing about.

title: 22  The Angular app
text:
22.5 Check the wiring yourself
Start with the folders, because every later page builds on them:
find frontend/src/app -type d
No page exists yet, so core/ is the folder that matters. The service and its test sit in it. A service in src/app itself means the agent skipped the layout bullets in AGENTS.md. Send it back to them before you prompt for the first page, because that page goes under features/ and has to find the service where the layout says it is.
Three claims from the prompt are easy to verify and easy for an agent to get half right. Start with the proxy and the mechanism.
find frontend -name "proxy.conf.*" -not -path "*/node_modules/*"
grep -rn "httpResource" frontend/src
The first command finds the proxy config, because the scaffold decides where it sits: next to angular.json in some runs, under src/ in others. Open the file it prints. It has to map /api to the port the backend actually listens on. So compare it against your launch settings instead of trusting the file.
The second grep is the decisive test in this chapter. It has to hit inside the service. And the hits have to be the stored-data reads: the list and the single value. A green gate proves the frontend compiles and the service tests pass. A page that shows the right numbers proves the requests arrive. Only this grep proves the reads went through the API you asked for instead of the one the model knows better.
If the grep comes back empty, the agent built the service out of HttpClient and observables and reported success. Send it back with the same two bullets, and add that the previous attempt used observables for the reads.
The third claim is that no component makes a request of its own. Look at where the requests come from:
grep -rn "HttpClient\|httpResource\|fetch(" frontend/src/app --include=*.ts
Two kinds of line are allowed in that output. Everything from the service file is allowed, because making requests is its job. provideHttpClient() in the application config is allowed too, because it’s the registration the service needs. Anything else is a component talking to the backend on its own. The values page chapter turns this rough grep into a check worth keeping. For now, confirm that the requests all live in one file.

title: 22  The Angular app
section: 22.6 Look at it in the browser
text:
22.6 Look at it in the browser
cd frontend
npm start
Open http://localhost:4200 on your machine. What you get is the page Angular scaffolds by default, since nothing has been built on top of it yet. That’s the point: the toolchain runs, and the browser reaches it. Stop the server with Ctrl+C when you’re done. A dev server left running holds port 4200, and the next run fails to bind it.






Getting to that port from your host



compose.yaml publishes port 4200, so localhost:4200 in your host browser reaches the dev server inside the container. If the page doesn’t load, the dev server is listening on the container’s own loopback address only. Start it with npm start -- --host 0.0.0.0 and try again.
Port 4200 and the backend port are the only published ones. For anything else, the Ports panel in the attached VS Code window forwards a port for you. Forward a Port adds one by hand, when it doesn’t appear there by itself.

title: 23  The calculations page
text: 23.1 The prompt

title: 23  The calculations page
text:
Add a calculations page to the frontend, with tests.

- The page shows a form with two number inputs. On submit it calls the backend
  add endpoint through the API service and displays the result.
- The result is displayed in green when it is >= 0 and in red when it is < 0.
- That red/green decision must live in an Angular pipe, not in the component.
- Test the pipe with Vitest.

Then add a stage to scripts/quality-gate.sh that runs the frontend Vitest tests
once, without watch mode. Commit when the quality gate is green.

title: 23  The calculations page
section: 23.2 Why the color rule has to live in a pipe
text:
23.2 Why the color rule has to live in a pipe
The third bullet looks like a style preference, but it’s not. Testability is a design constraint, and you are the one who has to impose it.
Put the red/green decision in a template expression, and the only way to check it is a component test or a browser. Both are slow, and slow checks stay outside the per-turn loop. Put the same decision in a pipe, and it becomes a pure function that takes a number and returns a class name. It comes with a Vitest test that runs in milliseconds. That test fits inside the gate, so it runs after every single agent turn.
Where you put logic decides which loop can check it. That’s the whole argument, and it applies far beyond Angular pipes.

title: 23  The calculations page
text:
23.3 Break it
You’ve added two gate stages in this step, the production build and Vitest. So far, you have only the agent’s word that either one works. Prove it the same way you proved the analyzer and the migrations drift check: make the gate fail on purpose.
Find the pipe spec first, since the agent chose its name:
grep -rln "green" frontend/src --include=*.spec.ts
Open the spec file it prints and change one expected green to red. Then run the gate by hand:
bash scripts/quality-gate.sh
tail -1 quality-gate.log
The last line has to read QUALITY GATE: RED, and the failing Vitest assertion has to be visible in quality-gate.log. Revert your edit, run it again, and confirm the gate is green before you move on.






A Vitest stage without a no-watch flag hangs



This break-it run matters more than the earlier ones. Vitest defaults to watch mode in some setups. A watch-mode stage inside the gate doesn’t fail. It just waits. A hanging stage looks exactly like a slow stage until somebody sits there for ten minutes wondering why the gate never finishes. Reading the script tells you nothing here. The flag may be correct, and the installed Vitest version may still behave differently. Only running it does.

title: 24  The values page
text: 24.1 The prompt

title: 24  The values page
text:
Add a Values page to the frontend.

- One single page that can create a Values entry, list all entries, fetch one by
  id (showing both numbers and their sum), and delete one.
- Everything happens on that one page. No routing between sub-views.
- All backend access goes through the existing API service. Do not add an HTTP
  call in a component.
- Reuse the existing styling approach, plain CSS with custom properties.

Commit when the quality gate is green.

title: 24  The values page
text:
24.2 Check for bypasses
The third bullet is the one to watch. Some agents cannot decide which method of the service to call. Others find it quicker to write the request right where it’s needed. Either way, the agent quietly injects HttpClient into the component instead. The page works and the gate stays green. The convention your api-access skill describes now protects nothing, because the requests no longer come from one place. Look for that directly.
Start by finding the service, since the agent chose where it lives:
grep -rln "httpResource" frontend/src/app --include=*.ts
Then list every place in the app that makes a request:
grep -rn "inject(HttpClient)\|httpResource\|fetch(" frontend/src/app --include=*.ts
Now look at what that second command deliberately does not search for. A bare HttpClient pattern would also match provideHttpClient() in app.config.ts. That call is not a bypass at all, it’s the registration the service itself needs to work. So the pattern asks for inject(HttpClient), which is how a component actually obtains one.
One legitimate hit is left, and it’s the loudest one. The service file matches every pattern in the list. It should, because making requests is its whole job. Drop it from the results:
grep -rn "inject(HttpClient)\|httpResource\|fetch(" frontend/src/app --include=*.ts \
  | grep -v "<the service file your first grep found>"
Anything still printed is a component talking to the backend on its own. Read it, then make the agent move that call into the service.
A check that accuses correct code gets ignored within a week. An ignored check is worse than no check. It still costs time, and it teaches you that the gate can be skipped. Narrowing has a price, though, and you just paid it: a component that takes HttpClient through its constructor never says inject(. So this pattern never catches it. Widen it the day your agent starts writing constructors.
Every check you add to this harness goes through the same process. Ask what correct code it would accuse, and narrow it until the answer is nothing.

title: 25  Playwright and tiers
text: 25.1 The prompt

title: 25  Playwright and tiers
text:
Add end-to-end tests with Playwright.

- Set up Playwright in the frontend project, latest stable version, Chromium only.
- One e2e test for the calculations page: enter two numbers, submit, check the
  result and that it is shown in the right color. Cover a negative result too.
- One e2e test for the values page: create a Values entry, see it in the list,
  open it by id and check the sum, then delete it.
- The tests need a running backend and a running frontend. Make that reproducible
  with npm scripts so one command runs the whole e2e suite. Name them
  `test:e2e` and `test:e2e:install`, and have the install script pass
  `--with-deps`.

Do NOT add Playwright to scripts/quality-gate.sh. These tests are far too slow to
run after every agent turn.

Keep your context small: read only the reference files you actually need.
Commit when the quality gate is green.

title: 25  Playwright and tiers
text:
25.2 What webServer does for you
Read frontend/playwright.config.ts when the run finishes. The webServer block is the part that matters. Playwright starts the backend and the Angular dev server, then waits until both answer. After the suite runs, it shuts both down again. You never have to start two processes in two terminals, and nothing stays running afterward.
The webServer block is what makes an end-to-end suite reproducible. Suppose a suite passes only after a person starts the backend and the frontend by hand. Then it fails in CI, with an error nobody can reproduce locally.

title: 25  Playwright and tiers
text:
25.3 Run the suite
cd frontend
npm run test:e2e:install   # once: Chromium plus system dependencies
npm run test:e2e
The install script runs once per container, because it downloads a browser and its system libraries. The suite itself prints something close to this:
Running 3 tests using 1 worker
  ok calculations page > adds two positive numbers and shows the sum in the success colour
  ok calculations page > shows a negative sum in the danger colour
  ok values page > creates a row, opens it by id, checks the sum and deletes it
  3 passed (9.0s)
Your run may have two tests or three, depending on how the agent split them. The names will be its own. They all have to pass.
Nine seconds sounds fast. Add the browser download, a dotnet build, two server startups, and a real database. The total is too slow for a check after every agent turn. That’s why this suite stays out of the gate script.

title: 25  Playwright and tiers
text:
25.4 Your gate now has tiers
Leaving Playwright out of scripts/quality-gate.sh was a design decision, and you just made it. Your checks now sit in tiers.








Loop
What runs
When




Per agent turn (agent_end)
format, analysis, unit and integration tests, migrations drift, frontend build, Vitest
automatically, every turn


On demand
Playwright end-to-end tests
when a human or the agent asks


Later
CI, deployment checks
on push



A check belongs in the per-turn loop if it’s fast enough that nobody is ever tempted to skip it. Make the gate slow and someone skips it. A skipped check protects nothing.

title: 25  Playwright and tiers
text:
25.5 What this step taught you
One gate, two toolchains. scripts/quality-gate.sh now drives dotnet and npm and still returns a single exit code.
Nothing cheap gates the contract. The TypeScript types in your API service and the C# on the other side describe the same requests twice, by hand. No tool compares the two. The Vitest tests for the service cannot see it either. HttpTestingController replaces the backend with one you invented in the test. So those tests prove the service builds the URL and the body you expect. But they run against a backend that always agrees. Rename a field in C# and every one of them still passes.
The values page end-to-end test is the only check in this project that drives the real chain, from the browser through Angular and .NET to Postgres. So the contract between your two toolchains is covered exactly once, in the slowest tier you own. That’s a decision rather than an accident: catching contract drift costs a browser and two servers, and nothing cheaper can do it. Know which tier holds your only check for a given failure, because that’s the tier you have to keep running.
Limit what the agent reads. The angular-developer skill ships 40 reference files. A small model that reads them all fills its context window with documentation and has nothing left for your task. That’s why the Playwright prompt tells it to read only the reference files it needs.

title: 26  Write a skill
text:
26.1 The procedure lives in your head
You built a Playwright end-to-end suite in the frontend part, and one npm script runs the whole thing. But that knowledge is not written down anywhere an agent will find it. You know which command starts the suite. You know that the backend and the Angular dev server both have to answer before the first test runs. You also know what to do when a port is still held by a server you forgot to stop. All of it lives in your head, and in a README nobody loads.
Ask an agent to “run the e2e tests” and it improvises. It starts a server here and forgets to stop one there. A stray dotnet run holds port 5074 for the rest of the afternoon.
A skill is where a procedure like that belongs. You have installed ten of them by now, and the chapter “The cutoff problem” showed how they load: the description sits in the agent’s context on every turn, and the body only when a task matches. So the body can be as long and as specific as the procedure really is.
The agent has also written one for you already. The Angular prompt in the frontend part asked for an api-access skill as one bullet in a long list. Now write one deliberately, as the whole task.

title: 26  Write a skill
text:
26.2 The prompt
Write a project skill that describes how to run the end-to-end tests: starting the
backend, starting the frontend, running the Playwright suite, and stopping
everything again afterward.

Read the `writing-for-agents` skill first and follow it. This document is written
for an agent, not for a human.

Put it in .agents/skills/e2e-tests/SKILL.md. Commit when the quality gate is green.
The second paragraph is what changes the output. Drop it and you get a README: background, then the command you need buried in the middle. The prompt sends the agent to writing-for-agents and tells it who the reader is. That turns the output into a document an agent can follow.

title: 26  Write a skill
section: 26.3 Read it like a harness engineer
text:
26.3 Read it like a harness engineer
Open .agents/skills/e2e-tests/SKILL.md and check it for four things. The examples below show what good looks like. Yours will read differently, so use them as the standard, not as the expected answer.
A description that names the situations. The description is the only part of a skill that sits in the agent’s context on every turn. It decides whether the body is ever opened. A description that says what the skill is fires when the agent happens to think of it. A description that names the situations fires when those situations happen. A good one ends with something like “and when a run fails because a URL is already used by a leftover server”. That is a second situation, and a less obvious one. Read your description and ask which situations would make an agent open this file. If the only answer is “when someone asks to run the e2e tests”, it is too narrow.
Steps with completion criteria. Not “run the tests”, but “done when the exit code is 0 and the list reporter shows every test passed”. An agent needs to know when it is finished. If you do not tell it, it decides for itself and usually stops too early.
A failure section. An agent can often improvise a success path but not a recovery path. That’s why failure modes are the part of a skill it cannot invent. A good one documents the “port already used” case together with its fix, pkill -f 'ng serve'. This is the item most likely to be missing from your file. Your agent wrote the skill without ever watching the suite fail, so it had nothing to document. An absent failure section is a finding. Write the section yourself from what you know, or ask for it in a follow-up prompt.
Rationale for the constraints. Whatever constraints your Playwright config carries, the skill has to say why they are there. A skill that only repeats a setting adds nothing the config file does not already say. If your config pins one worker, the skill owes you the reason. A good one reads: “Sequential by design (workers: 1): the tests share the real database.” Yours may run more workers and carry different constraints. The same question applies to each of them. Without the why, a future agent helpfully turns parallelism back on and the tests fight over the same rows. You then spend an afternoon on intermittent failures.






Compare the e2e skill with the api-access skill



Open .agents/skills/api-access/SKILL.md, the one the Angular prompt asked for. One file describes a procedure, and the other describes a convention. Both are useful for the same reason. They say when they apply and how the thing they cover fails.


Fix what the review finds before you move on. A skill you have read and corrected is one you can start calling on purpose.

title: 26  Write a skill
text:
26.4 Force it and watch
A skill normally loads when the agent decides it is relevant. Forcing it is how you find out whether the one you just wrote works. In pi, type:
/skill:e2e-tests
Whatever you type after the command name is handed to the skill as the request:
/skill:e2e-tests only the values spec
You watch the agent follow your own steps instead of guessing whether the description would have fired. Where it improvises, the skill is missing a step. Fix the file, run /reload so the session picks up the change, and force it again. The forced skill also turns a procedure into a command you can call by name instead of a document you have to reread.

title: 26  Write a skill
text:
26.5 What this step taught you
Skills are how a harness remembers procedures. AGENTS.md loads on every turn, so it can only hold what is always true. A skill loads when it becomes relevant, so it can carry detail that would be waste in AGENTS.md: the exact commands, the failure modes, and the reason each constraint exists.
The description decides whether the skill is read. A perfect procedure behind a vague description does nothing, so spend your editing time on the one line that sits in context on every turn.
The harness now writes parts of itself. You used an agent, guided by a skill about writing for agents, to write a skill for agents. The agent produced a draft, and you made it complete by checking it against the four things a skill needs: triggers in the description, completion criteria in the steps, a failure section, and rationale for the constraints.
The frontend still has no gate. The backend has had a formatter and a static analyzer since the quality gate part, and the frontend has neither. That is the next thing to fix, and then you can measure what the whole gate costs you.

title: 27  Lint the frontend
text:
27.1 The prompt
The backend has had a formatter and a static analyzer since you built the quality gate. The frontend has had neither. The Angular app, the calculations page, the values page, and the Playwright suite are all written by the agent. A build and a few Vitest runs are the only checks on them. Nothing in scripts/quality-gate.sh checks how that TypeScript looks or which patterns it uses.
This chapter adds ESLint and Prettier to the frontend. It also adds a lint and format stage to scripts/quality-gate.sh. That completes the harness. The next chapter measures what the full gate costs to run after every agent turn.
Start pi and paste this:

title: 27  Lint the frontend
text:
Add linting and formatting to the Angular frontend.

Follow https://www.angulararchitects.io/en/blog/best-practices-prettier-eslint/
but keep it simple: this is a teaching project, not a production app.

- ESLint for TypeScript and Angular templates, Prettier for formatting.
- The two must not fight each other about formatting.
- npm scripts to check and to fix.
- Add a stage to scripts/quality-gate.sh that runs the lint and the format check.

Then prove the gate works: introduce a formatting problem and an ESLint violation
in one frontend file, run the gate, confirm it turns red, then fix them and get it
back to green.

Keep your context small: read only what you actually need.
Commit when the quality gate is green.

title: 27  Lint the frontend
text:
27.2 Two bullets prevent two failures
“The two must not fight each other about formatting.” ESLint and Prettier overlap. Both have opinions about where a line breaks and how many spaces sit in front of it. Wire them together naively and you get rules that undo each other. Prettier writes a line one way. An ESLint layout rule reports it as wrong. You fix it for ESLint, and the next format run puts it back. That gate can never turn green. The usual fix is a config that turns off ESLint’s layout rules and leaves formatting to Prettier, but check what your agent actually did. Naming the conflict in the prompt is much cheaper than debugging it afterward.
“Then prove the gate works.” You have already broken the analyzer gate, the migrations drift check, and the database container, all on purpose. A gate you’ve never seen fail is a gate you’re guessing about. So the prompt tells the agent to do the breaking. The next chapter asks you to repeat it yourself: the agent claiming red is not the same as you watching red.

title: 27  Lint the frontend
section: 27.3 Expect a big diff either way
text:
27.3 Expect a big diff either way
Turning Prettier on for the first time reformats the whole frontend. The diff touches nearly every file the agent has ever written there. ESLint finds problems in code that was written before it existed: unused imports and any where a type belonged. Some runs split the result into two commits, configuration first and cleanup second. Others land everything in one. Either way, the reformat noise and the real fixes arrive together. That is exactly why you read the commit list before the diff.
Check what actually landed:
git log --oneline -5
git show --stat HEAD
Look for a commit whose stat block lists most of the frontend, with only one or two changed lines per file. That commit is the Prettier sweep, and the pattern is normal, not a sign that something went wrong. What you don’t want is a single commit that mixes the reformat with a behavior change. Then nobody can review either half. If the agent produced that, say so and ask it to split them.
Once the gate is green, go read what the agent added to scripts/quality-gate.sh.

title: 28  Check, never fix
text:
28.1 Count the stages
The agent says the frontend lint stage is in. Go look.
scripts/quality-gate.sh most likely has a helper that runs one stage and prints a header. Open the script and find out what yours is called before you grep for anything. A common name is run_stage, but your agent may have named it run_step or plain step instead. Some agents skip the helper for one stage and write it inline. No single grep pattern fits every script.
The count you are after is in the log, not in the script. Every stage prints a header when it runs, so run the gate and count the headers:
Adjust the pattern to match your script’s headers. Run tail -50 of the log to see what they look like. The exact count is the agent’s choice, not a target. One run bundles ESLint and Prettier into a single stage. Another gives npm ci a stage of its own. Match each header in the log to a check you added on purpose. Look for a stage you cannot explain, or a check that never got a stage, and chase that down before you go on.
dotnet and npm are two different ecosystems, but they run behind the same entry point: one script. The extension calls that script. So does your shell, and one day a CI job will too. None of them needs to know anything about either toolchain.

title: 28  Check, never fix
text:
bash scripts/quality-gate.sh
grep -c "^=== " quality-gate.log

title: 28  Check, never fix
section: 28.2 The npm scripts come in pairs
text:
28.2 The npm scripts come in pairs
Open frontend/package.json and read the scripts block. The lint and format entries come in pairs, one that reports and one that repairs. They look something like this, even if your names differ:
"lint": "eslint .",
"lint:fix": "eslint . --fix",
"format": "prettier --write .",
"format:check": "prettier --check ."
Now check which half of each pair the gate calls. It has to be the checking half.
A gate that silently fixes your code hides the very thing it was built to reveal. It also makes the agent’s work look cleaner than it was. The agent writes badly formatted TypeScript. The gate reformats it and reports green. You never learn that the agent needs a stronger instruction. The evidence is gone, erased by the thing that was supposed to collect it.
This is the same reason the backend stage runs dotnet format --verify-no-changes instead of plain dotnet format. Report, don’t repair. If your agent wired format or lint:fix into the script, change it now.

title: 28  Check, never fix
text:
28.3 Settling the indentation conflict
The backend indents with 4 spaces. Prettier defaults to 2 for TypeScript. The conflict only bites once two toolchains share a repository. Both .editorconfig and .prettierrc set indentation rules, and they can disagree.
There are at least two reasonable answers:

A scoped section in .editorconfig, something like [frontend/**], that gives the frontend its own 2-space rule.
Letting .prettierrc control everything under frontend/ and leaving .editorconfig for the backend.

Your agent may have picked either. What you’re checking is that somebody decided, not which one they decided. The failure mode is the case where nobody decided. Two tools quietly overwrite each other’s indentation, and one file flips back and forth between 2 and 4 spaces depending on which tool ran last. The gate catches that as a format check that fails forever, no matter how often you run the fixer. Knowing why is much faster than bisecting your config files.

title: 28  Check, never fix
text:
28.4 Break it yourself
Don’t just believe what the agent says. Mangle one line:
# put some random extra spaces into a frontend .ts file, then:
bash scripts/quality-gate.sh
tail -1 quality-gate.log
The log looks roughly like this, with your own file name:
=== Stage: frontend lint (ESLint) + format check (Prettier) ===
[warn] src/app/calculations/result-color.pipe.spec.ts
[warn] Code style issues found in the above file. Run Prettier with --write to fix.
RESULT: FAIL (exit code 1)

QUALITY GATE: RED
The stage header and the Prettier wording depend on how your agent wrote the script. QUALITY GATE: RED and exit code 1 are the stable part. Those are what the extension and any future CI job read. Then git checkout the file and run the gate again. Confirm it comes back GREEN.

title: 28  Check, never fix
text:
28.5 One file, two verdicts
Read the rest of the gate log, not just the last line. The Vitest stage passed for the same file, in the same run, while the format check failed on it. The code was correct and badly formatted at the same time. The harness said so, in one sentence each.
The gate carries this many stages because different stages answer different questions. Vitest answers “does the logic work.” Prettier answers “is it formatted.” ESLint checks whether the code follows our conventions. None of the three can replace the others. You need all of them, and the next chapter is about what that costs.

title: 29  Count the cost
text:
29.1 The honest questions
The harness is finished, and it has a real price. Every stage in scripts/quality-gate.sh runs after every agent turn. That means you pay for all of them every time the agent stops to think. Time a full run:
Write the number down. That number is the tax on every turn from here on.
Now ask the questions you would ask about anyone else’s build:
A harness you dread is a harness you disable. Here is the usual path on a real team. The pre-commit hook gets slower. Somebody discovers --no-verify. Within a month the gate protects nothing, because nobody runs it. A fast gate is a gate people keep running.

title: 29  Count the cost
text:
Which stages could run only when the files they care about changed? Nothing in the frontend moved, so ESLint had nothing to do. The script could ask git which files changed since the last green run. Then it could skip the stages those files cannot affect.
Does npm ci need to run on every gate invocation? It reinstalls the whole dependency tree from package-lock.json. That lock file changes maybe once a week. The install only matters when that file changed.
Which stage is slowest, and is it worth the time? Not every slow stage is wasted time. The integration tests are slow because they talk to a real database. That is the whole point of them. Cut the stage that is slow and catches little.
Which stages should move to CI? Playwright already showed you the tiering pattern: fast checks belong in the per-turn loop, slow checks run on demand only, and everything else waits for a push. Any check you skip belongs in a slower tier.

title: 29  Count the cost
text:
29.2 What this step taught you
A gate checks and never fixes. --check and --verify-no-changes exist so that a gate reports instead of repairing. An auto-fixing gate destroys the evidence you built it to collect. It tells you the code was fine, when really the gate just fixed it.
Coverage is a series of deliberate choices. Look at what the stages actually cover now:



Question
Stage




Does it compile?
dotnet build


Does it follow our conventions?
analyzers, ESLint


Is it formatted?
dotnet format, Prettier


Does the logic work?
xUnit, Vitest


Does it work against a real database?
integration tests


Are generated artifacts current?
migrations drift check


Does the whole stack work?
Playwright, on demand



Nobody planned that table in advance, including you. Each row got added the moment your harness let something through: a build that passed with sloppy formatting, an entity that changed without a migration, a test suite that never touched Postgres. Real harnesses get built one leak at a time.

title: 29  Count the cost
text:
29.3 What you actually did here
You spent six steps on this project and wrote almost no application code. The agent wrote the app. You built the machine that decides whether the app is acceptable. You broke every part of that machine on purpose, before you trusted any of it.
You now have a harness you can defend. You know what each stage catches, and you know what the whole run costs.

title: 29  Count the cost
text:
29.4 Where to take it next
You have a working harness in front of you. Here are three next steps.
Take the slow tier to CI. Playwright is the only check you own that drives the real chain from the browser to Postgres. That makes it the only check that would catch your frontend and backend disagreeing about a field name. Right now it runs when somebody remembers. Put it in a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on every push. At the same time, take the slowest stage from your timing run out of the per-turn loop. You have already made the tiering decision once, so the second time goes faster.
Gate a generated artifact in your own project. The migrations drift check works because you can ask EF Core whether the generated file still matches its source. Go find the equivalent in the next project you touch. Something produced each one: a lock file, a snapshot test, generated TypeScript, a compiled schema. You can ask whether it is still current, and that answer belongs in the gate.
Build the same harness around a stronger model. Everything here ran on GPT-6 Luna, a low-cost model, on purpose. A small model trips the gates often enough that you can watch each one catch a failure. At home, point a stronger agent at your next project and give it the same treatment: an AGENTS.md with the rules, a skill for each procedure, one gate script, and a hook that runs it after every turn. A better model writes better code. It does not tell you whether the code is acceptable. That part is still your job.

title: Appendix A — Troubleshooting
text:
Something will misbehave. When it does, look for the symptom in the left column before you read your own code. Almost everything that breaks in this course is a harness problem, not a code problem: an extension never loaded, a stopped container, a trust prompt nobody accepted. The application code is usually fine. You fix the harness around it.







Symptom
Cause and fix




pi reports an authentication error
auth.json next to compose.yaml is missing, is malformed, or holds the activity code instead of your key. A key starts with nvk-. Check the JSON shape against the example in the “Your toolkit” chapter, and open the activity page again to read your key. The page always hands back the same one, so a key that stops working means your teacher closed the activity.


pi fails with a confusing configuration error on first start
auth.json did not exist when the container first started, so Docker created a directory under that name. On your host, in the folder that holds compose.yaml: docker compose down, delete the auth.json directory, run cp auth.json.example auth.json and paste your key in, then docker compose up -d.


pi will not start, and node reports an error about a bootloader script
VS Code’s JavaScript auto-attach sets NODE_OPTIONS=--require .../bootloader.js in the terminals it opens, and pi fails to start with it. Run unset NODE_OPTIONS in that terminal, then start pi again. Auto-attach is a setting in your own VS Code rather than something in the container, so turn it off with the command Debug: Toggle Auto Attach if it keeps coming back.


Agent does not know about microsoft-docs
The project is not trusted. Restart pi and accept the trust prompt, or start it with pi -a.


ls ~/skill-source prints nothing
The skill-source/ folder was not next to compose.yaml when the container started, so Docker mounted an empty directory instead. Put the folder from your teacher back next to compose.yaml, then run docker compose up -d again


dotnet test rejects a flag such as --nologo
xUnit v3 runs on the Microsoft Testing Platform, which refuses some flags the older VSTest runner accepted. Current packages work this way by design, so your code is not the problem. Let the agent read the error and adjust the test invocation in the gate script.


dotnet format fails on files under the migrations folder
The EF Core migration generator writes files the formatter and analyzers dislike, starting with a byte order mark. Add a scoped .editorconfig section for the migrations folder. Check that the scope covers that folder and nothing more. See the “The harness pays off” chapter.


Build warning MSB3277 (conflicting assembly versions) in the test project
The Npgsql provider’s dependency ranges can pull different versions into the API and test projects. TreatWarningsAsErrors turns that warning into a red gate. Let the agent align the package versions across both projects.


The gate never runs by itself
The extension has to exist before the session starts, so the session that wrote it never loaded it. Restart pi or run /reload. Then check the timestamp on quality-gate.log after the next turn.


The gate still never runs after a restart
Project-local extensions only load in a trusted project, and only from .pi/extensions/. Accept the trust prompt or start with pi -a. Then check where the file landed.


The gate goes red and the agent stops anyway
The extension is listening on agent_settled instead of agent_end. A message on agent_settled never starts a new turn. See the “Automate the gate” chapter.


npx @microsoft/learn-cli is slow the first time
The first call downloads the package. Later calls use the cache.


Agent runs out of context while reading quality-gate.log
The log gets long. Tell the agent to read only the tail, or make the gate script log a summary.


A run went badly wrong
Run git checkout . and git clean -fd, then rephrase the prompt. Resetting is cheaper than arguing with the agent.


Gate red with NpgsqlException
The db container is not running. Run docker compose start db on your host.


dotnet ef not found
Rebuild the container with docker compose build dev. Or let the agent add a local tool manifest and run dotnet tool restore.


Integration tests fail only in a full run
They assume an empty database, and they share that database with the app. See the “Integration tests” chapter.


pi prints nothing for several minutes
A request to the shared endpoint was lost. Abort and send the same prompt again. It usually succeeds. Run only one pi session at a time, because concurrent sessions lose requests more often.


This extension ctx is stale after session replacement or reload, and pi dies
The gate extension’s agent_end handler returns before it has sent its message, so the gate talks to a session that has already been replaced. The handler has to await the gate and send the message before returning. See the “Automate the gate” chapter.


The agent keeps retrying a gate it cannot fix
Nothing limits the number of retries, and the gate stays red for a reason outside the code. Limit the consecutive retries. See the “Close the loop” chapter.


Author identity unknown when the agent commits
You never set git config user.name and git config user.email. See the “Git is your undo button” chapter.


Playwright says “port is already used”
A previous run ended without releasing the port. Run pkill -f 'ng serve' and pkill -f 'backend/Calculator.Api'.


Agent uses up its context on documentation
The angular-developer skill ships 40 reference files. Tell the agent to read only what it needs.


~/work is empty and everything is gone
Somebody ran docker compose down -v, which deletes the work_data volume that holds it. Plain docker compose down and a rebuild both keep it. See the note in the “Git is your undo button” chapter.


The API responds inside the container, but your browser cannot reach port 5074
Check whether the API listens only on the container’s loopback address. Ask the agent to set applicationUrl to http://0.0.0.0:5074 in the launchSettings.json profile used by dotnet run. Restart the API and retry from your browser. compose.yaml already publishes port 5074.


Browser cannot reach the app’s port
compose.yaml publishes only ports 4200 and 5074. For any other port, use the VS Code Ports panel in the attached window to forward it.


git checkout . did not undo the run
git checkout . only reverts tracked files. The agent’s new files stay until you run git clean -fd.
